title: To You, 10,000 Qubits From Now
excerpt: Inside the Most Ambitious Resource Estimate for Quantum Factoring Ever Published
text: Inside the Most Ambitious Resource Estimate for Quantum Factoring Ever Published !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1fECLrsjke0RZxozcirLgWg.png This is Part 4 of my series on Shor’s algorithm and the state of quantum factoring. Part 1: “Sometimes its too slow…,For Shorhttps://medium.com/@monitsharma/sometimes-its-too-slow-for-shor-c01677032324”, established that current hardware can barely factor 15. Part 2: “The Emperor Has No Factors”https://medium.com/@monitsharma/the-emperor-has-no-factors-9eaec0d9bd0d showed that most published quantum factoring claims can’t survive a null-baseline test. Part 3: “The Fault in Our Qubits”https://medium.com/@monitsharma/the-fault-in-our-qubits-8c66ef11f0c5 quantified the engineering gap between today’s machines and cryptographically relevant factoring. This post examines a new paper that claims to dramatically narrow that gap. On March 31, 2026 — after I published Part 3 of this series about the vast engineering chasm separating current quantum hardware from useful factoring — a team from Oratomichttps://www.oratomic.com/ and Caltech dropped a paper claiming Shor’s algorithm is possible with “as few as 10,000 reconfigurable atomic qubits.”https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28627v1 Ten thousand. In Part 3, I anchored my scaling analysis to Gidney’s 2025 estimate of roughly one million qubits for RSA-2048 factoring, noting Webster et al.’s 2026 Pinnacle architecture had pushed that down to around 100,000 qubits with quantum LDPC codes. The trajectory was clear: the number was falling, but the gap to reality remained enormous. Now Cain, Xu, King, and collaborators — a team including John Preskillhttps://scholar.google.com/citations?user=K2BMBtcAAAAJ&hl=en and several researchers behind some of the most important neutral-atom quantum computing results of the past three years — are claiming another order-of-magnitude reduction. If true, this would place the qubit count for breaking real cryptography within shouting distance of systems that have already been demonstrated in the lab, at least in raw qubit count. That’s an extraordinary claim. It deserves extraordinary scrutiny. Here’s the punchline up front: the paper contains genuinely impressive theoretical contributions in quantum error-correcting code construction, architecture design, and compilation. The authors are transparent about their assumptions to a degree that is, frankly, refreshing. But the “10,000 qubits” headline, the number that will circulate on social media, get cited in policy briefs, and alarm cryptographers, tells a story that the paper’s own tables contradict. The full picture is more nuanced, more interesting, and more honest than the headline. Let’s read the fine print. What the Paper Actually Claims The paper, “Shor’s algorithm is possible with as few as 10,000 reconfigurable atomic qubits,” proposes fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures built on reconfigurable neutral-atom arrays. The core technical contributions are: 1. High-rate quantum error-correcting codes. The authors develop new constructions of lifted-product LP codes with encoding rates of approximately 30%, meaning roughly 30% of the physical qubits carry logical information, compared to about 4% for the bi-variate bicycle codes used in other recent proposals, and effectively less than 1% for surface codes. They present three main memory codes: a \\2610, 744, ≤16\\ code, a \\4350, 1224, ≤20\\ code, and a \\5278, 1480, ≤24\\ code. These are substantial codes, encoding over a thousand logical qubits each, with extrapolated block error rates reaching 10⁻¹¹ per cycle at 0.1% physical error rates. 2. A zoned architecture. The proposed quantum computer is divided into four functional zones: a memory zone for storing logical qubits during computation, a processor zone for active computation on smaller code blocks, an operation zone containing ancilla qubits for performing code surgery the mechanism by which logical operations are executed, and a resource zone for generating the magic states needed for non-Clifford operations. This is a clean, modular design that leverages the reconfigurability of neutral-atom arrays — atoms can be physically moved between zones during computation. 3. A compilation strategy. Circuits are broken into sub-circuits that fit inside the processor code, teleported from memory to processor, computed upon, and teleported back. This is clever because it means the expensive code surgery operations scale with the processor code size, not the memory code size. 4. Resource estimates for RSA-2048 and ECC-256. The paper evaluates several architectures with different space-time tradeoffs, using state-of-the-art circuit constructions from the literature. So far, so good. The technical machinery is serious, the code constructions are novel, and the architecture is thoughtfully designed. Now let’s look at the numbers. The Headline vs. The Table: A Space-Time Tradeoff You Can’t Ignore Here is the central tension of this paper, laid out in the authors’ own data. The paper presents four classes of architecture for each cryptographic target. Let me reconstruct the key numbers from their Figure 3 and Extended Data Table IV: !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1kfQiESIdu4OWTnQ-5wbpQ.jpeg The “as few as 10,000 qubits” claim corresponds to the space-efficient ECC-256 architecture with 9,739 qubits. That’s technically correct. But the runtime for this architecture is approximately 1,000 days, nearly three years of continuously error-corrected, sustained fault-tolerant quantum computation. For the problem most people actually care about, RSA-2048; the 10,000-qubit regime means a runtime of 118 years. The more time-relevant scenarios in the paper, weeks to months rather than years or decades, require roughly 26,000 qubits for ECC-256 and 102,000 for RSA-2048, though the authors explicitly describe those time-efficient estimates as preliminary. These are still remarkable numbers, far below the million-qubit estimates that dominated the literature until recently. But they are not 10,000. This is not a minor distinction. The difference between “we need 10,000 qubits” and “we need 100,000 qubits” is the difference between a system that looks tantalizingly close to demonstrated capabilities 6,100 trapped atoms have been shown in a single arrayhttps://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09641-4 and one that requires significant further scaling. The paper is transparent about all of this, the tables are right there. But the title, abstract, and framing all lead with the small number. To be clear, the authors do note in the abstract that “increasing the number of physical qubits improves time efficiency by enabling greater parallelism” and provide the 26,000-qubit ECC-256 figure alongside the headline. The data is honestly presented. The framing choices, however, are worth examining. The Assumption Stack Every resource estimate is only as strong as its assumptions. This paper is built on several layers of assumptions, each of which deserves individual examination. I’ll organise them from most to least well-established. Assumption 1: 0.1% Physical Error Rates Across the Full System The paper’s code performance analysis assumes a uniform depolarizing noise model with physical error rate p = 0.1% on entangling gates, state preparations, and measurements. The most aggressive architectures require physical error rates as low as p = 0.048%. Where does current hardware stand? The paper itself cites Bluvstein et al. 2026https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09848-5, which demonstrated below-threshold fault-tolerant operation on systems of up to ~448 atoms, “with a path to 10× below threshold.” But below-threshold operation on hundreds of atoms is not the same as demonstrating the paper’s assumed ~0.1% physical error regime across a 10,000+ qubit system. The threshold depends on the code, decoder, circuit context, and noise model, it is not a simple conversion to a universal physical error rate number. Critically, high-fidelity entangling operations have only been demonstrated on regions of a few hundred qubits. The paper acknowledges this: “increasing laser power could directly enable operation on thousands of qubits.” But going from demonstrated fidelity at hundreds of qubits to sustained 0.1% error rates across 10,000+ qubits is not merely a matter of turning up the laser power. It requires maintaining coherence, calibration, and crosstalk suppression at a scale that hasn’t been attempted. The paper makes an interesting argument about duty cycle: current systems use continuous-wave lasers with only 0.1% duty cycle ~200 ns gates separated by ≥200 μs idle periods, and rastering the beam dynamically could increase the number of addressable atoms by three orders of magnitude. This is a plausible path. It is not a demonstrated capability. Verdict: The 0.1% assumption is aspirational but not unreasonable as a target for a purpose-built system. It requires a substantial improvement over current demonstrated fault-tolerant operation, extended from hundreds of active fault-tolerant qubits to systems in the 10,000+ range. The p = 0.048% required for some configurations is more aggressive still. Assumption 2: 1 ms Stabilizer Measurement Cycle Time The paper assumes a 1 ms cycle time for stabilizer measurements. Current neutral-atom systems require several milliseconds per cycle, bottlenecked by readout and atomic motion. The paper notes that “realizing this in practice may require technological development” — a diplomatic understatement. This assumption matters because, at fixed fault-tolerant workload, runtime scales roughly linearly with cycle time. As a simple sensitivity check: the 97-day RSA-2048 figure at 1 ms would stretch to roughly 970 days at 10 ms, or about 2.7 years. The 10-day ECC-256 estimate would become 100 days. These rescalings are mine, not the paper’s stated estimates, but they illustrate how sensitive the runtime numbers are to this single parameter. The paper’s outlook section discusses far more aggressive speedups: microsecond-scale readout reducing measurement times by 1000× and constant-velocity atom transport potentially hundreds of times faster. If even a fraction of these improvements materialize, the 1 ms assumption would be conservative. But these are future hardware developments, not current capabilities. Verdict: Optimistic but within reach. The 1 ms cycle time represents a moderate improvement over current systems, and the paper identifies concrete technical paths to achieving it. Assumption 3: Block Error Rate Extrapolations This is where things get more subtle. The paper’s resource estimates depend on extrapolating code performance to physical error rates that cannot be directly simulated. The extrapolation method is power-law fitting of the form y = ax^b, using data points from Monte Carlo simulations at higher error rates. The authors are commendably transparent about the limitations here. For two of their three memory codes lp₂₀ and lp₂₄, the fitted exponent b exceeds d/2, which is the theoretical maximum as p → 0. This means the standard fitting procedure produces unphysically optimistic extrapolations. The authors address this by conservatively fitting y = ax^d/2 from the single smallest simulated error rate — a reasonable correction, but one that means the extrapolated performance rests on a single data point. The lp₂₄ code’s extrapolated block error rate of ~10⁻¹¹ per cycle at p = 0.1% is what enables the extremely large Toffoli counts required for RSA-2048. If the actual performance at p = 0.1% is worse than extrapolated by even an order of magnitude, the required physical error rate tightens significantly. Verdict: The extrapolation methodology is standard in the field and the authors handle the anomalous fits responsibly. But extrapolating over an order of magnitude in error rate from a handful of data points introduces genuine uncertainty that is difficult to quantify. Assumption 4: Code Surgery Performance at Scale The paper’s compilation strategy relies on code surgery, a technique for performing logical measurements by temporarily merging code blocks with ancilla systems. The authors construct and numerically benchmark surgery gadgets for their smallest processor code the \\248, 10, ≤18\\ bivariate bicycle code, demonstrating that surgery error rates are within an order of magnitude of the code’s idling error rate. However, the larger surgery systems required for the balanced and time-efficient architectures are not numerically benchmarked. The paper states: “We expect similar behavior for the larger gadgets… and leave detailed simulations to future work.” The operation zone construction relies on an algebraic framework from an upcoming paper \113\ that provides low-weight logical operator bases for LP codes. This is a critical dependency on unpublished work. Verdict: The surgery framework is theoretically well-motivated and the small-scale benchmarks are encouraging. But the key resource cost estimates for larger architectures rest on extrapolation from small instances and unpublished constructions. Assumption 5: Time-Efficient Architecture Viability The most dramatic runtime reductions come from the “time-efficient” architectures, which assume highly parallel Toffoli gate execution. This requires: 1. Parallel high-rate code surgery measuring many logical operators simultaneously, which has been demonstrated on ~10 PPMs for distance-~10 codes. 2. Carry-lookahead adders replacing ripple-carry adders, reducing Toffoli depth from On to Olog n. 3. Factory codes encoding hundreds of logical qubits with 20–30% rates, referenced to codes in “upcoming work \125\.” The paper is explicit that these estimates are “preliminary and can be optimized in future work.” The parallel surgery techniques are referenced to prior work that has been benchmarked only at small scale. The carry-lookahead adder speedup estimate is computed as a proxy — the full circuit compilation has not been performed. Verdict: The time-efficient architecture is the least mature component of the paper. It represents a plausible roadmap rather than a concrete proposal. The Code Constructions: What’s Genuinely New With the caveats above established, let me give credit where it’s substantial. The lifted-product code constructions in this paper are a real contribution. The key insight is that reconfigurable atom arrays provide exactly the kind of non-local connectivity that high-rate qLDPC codes need. Surface codes, the workhorses of most prior resource estimates, achieve less than 1% encoding rate because they require only local nearest-neighbor connectivity. Bivariate bicycle codes, used in IBM’s recent work and in the Pinnacle architecture, achieve about 4% rates with slightly more connectivity. The LP codes in this paper achieve ~30% encoding rates by exploiting the fully nonlocal, reconfigurable connectivity of atom arrays. The numbers are striking. The lp₂₄ code \\5278, 1480, ≤24\\ encodes 1,480 logical qubits in 5,278 physical qubits. A surface code with the same distance and number of logical qubits would require 161× more physical qubits, roughly 850,000. That’s where most of the qubit savings come from. The codes are found using what the paper describes as an “LLM-assisted heuristic computer search” — an interesting methodological note suggesting that large language models were used in the code discovery process. The seed matrices for each code are explicitly provided Appendix A, which is important for reproducibility. The decoder design also leverages LLM-assisted search, using an ensemble of five belief propagation with localized statistics BP-LSD decoder instances, each operating under different noise assumptions. The ensemble approach, running decoders with optimistic, pessimistic, nominal, randomized, and perturbed probability models, is clever and practical. Where This Sits in the Resource Estimate Trajectory The paper’s Figure 1b tells a remarkable story. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/453/1cui60wl1uBxBF4nYjxnPQ.png Figure 1b from the paper. Resource estimates for cryptographically relevant Shor’s algorithm have dropped five orders of magnitude over two decades: - 2012 Jones et al.: ~10⁹ physical qubits - 2012 Fowler et al.: ~10⁸ physical qubits - 2017 O’Gorman & Campbell: ~10⁸ physical qubits - 2019 Gidney & Ekerå: ~2 × 10⁷ physical qubits - 2025 Gidney: ~10⁶ physical qubits - 2026 Webster et al.: ~10⁵ physical qubits with non-local connectivity - 2026 This work: ~10⁴ physical qubits most space-efficient to ~10⁵ time-efficient Each step down involves a different category of improvement. The early reductions came from better surface code constructions and magic state distillation. Gidney’s 2025 work optimized within the surface code paradigm to reach ~1 million qubits. Webster et al. introduced qLDPC codes with small block sizes ~10 logical qubits per block and quasi-local connectivity. This paper goes further with high-rate codes hundreds to thousands of logical qubits per block and fully nonlocal connectivity. The critical observation from my Part 3https://medium.com/@monitsharma/the-fault-in-our-qubits-8c66ef11f0c5 analysis still holds, but the landscape has shifted: the gap between “qubits demonstrated in a lab” and “qubits needed for cryptography” has narrowed from roughly four orders of magnitude to roughly one. But, and this is essential, narrowing the gap in qubit count does not proportionally narrow the gap in engineering difficulty. The 6,100-atom trapping array demonstrated by Manetsch et al. 2025 did not perform quantum computation. The fault-tolerant demonstrations by Bluvstein et al. 2026 achieved below-threshold operation on up to ~448 atoms, not the deep-below-threshold performance needed for the codes in this paper. Closing the remaining gap in qubit count while simultaneously achieving substantially better error rates across a far larger system, implementing novel code surgery protocols with only limited benchmarking so far, and sustaining all of this for days to months of continuous operation, that is a fundamentally different challenge than simply scaling up a trapping array. The Neutral-Atom Platform Argument This paper is, at its core, an argument for neutral-atom quantum computing as the platform most likely to achieve utility-scale fault-tolerant computation. The case rests on several genuine advantages: 1. Reconfigurability. Atoms can be physically moved during computation, enabling the non-local connectivity that high-rate codes require. This is a real structural advantage over superconducting qubits, which are fixed in place and limited to nearest-neighbor or short-range interactions. The paper’s entire architecture, with its memory, processor, operation, and resource zones, is designed around this mobility. 2. Identical qubits. Unlike superconducting qubits, which must be individually calibrated and whose parameters drift, neutral atoms are fundamentally identical. This simplifies error correction protocols and enables global parallel control. 3. Scalable trapping. Arrays of thousands of atoms have been demonstrated, and metasurface-based approaches could potentially scale to hundreds of thousands of traps. These are legitimate advantages. They are also not the whole story. Neutral-atom systems have significant disadvantages in clock speed millisecond-scale operations vs. microsecond-scale for superconducting systems, readout fidelity and speed, and the engineering complexity of maintaining a large-scale ultra-high-vacuum system with precision laser control over thousands of individual atoms for extended periods. The paper addresses clock speed by noting that hardware improvements microsecond readout, constant-velocity transport could eventually bring cycle times down by orders of magnitude. The outlook section even suggests that “runtimes on the scale of hours or even minutes” could be achievable with sufficient hardware development. These are aspirational projections, not engineering commitments, and should be understood as such. The Conflict of Interest Question All nine authors of this paper are shareholders of Oratomic, Inc. Six are full-time employees, and three including John Preskill and Manuel Endres are part-time employees. Oratomic is developing fault-tolerant neutral-atom quantum computers. The paper concludes that “appropriately designed neutral-atom architectures could support cryptographically relevant implementations of Shor’s algorithm” — a conclusion directly aligned with Oratomic’s business thesis. I want to be precise about what this does and does not mean. It does not mean the results are wrong. The technical contributions, the code constructions, the decoder design, the architecture, are presented with sufficient detail for independent verification. The authors are transparent about their affiliations, their assumptions, and the limitations of their estimates. The paper explicitly uses phrases like “substantial engineering challenges remain,” “although realizing this in practice may require technological development,” and “we emphasize that these estimates are preliminary.” What it does mean is that the framing choices, which number goes in the title, which runtime gets emphasized, how the comparison to existing hardware is drawn, should be read with awareness of this alignment. “10,000 qubits” in the title rather than “26,000 to 102,000 qubits for time-relevant scenarios” is a framing choice. It’s not dishonest, the 10,000-qubit architecture exists in their analysis, but it is the most optimistic credible framing of their results. This does not invalidate the analysis, but it does raise the importance of separating what the calculations show from how the results are packaged. In the quantum computing space, these framing choices matter. The strongest version of this paper, the one most useful to the research community, leads with the space-time tradeoff matrix, not the minimum qubit count. What This Means for Cryptographic Risk Throughout this series, I’ve been tracking how close quantum computers are to breaking real-world cryptography. Let me update the assessment with this paper’s data. ECC-256 elliptic curve cryptography: This is the more immediate target. The paper’s most credible attack scenario, the time-efficient architecture with ~26,000 qubits and ~10 days, requires: - 26,000 physical qubits at 0.1% error rates, sustained for 10 continuous days - A 1 ms cycle time - Fully functional parallel high-rate code surgery at scale - Carry-look-ahead adder circuits that have been compiled but not fully benchmarked in this framework If all assumptions are met, ECC-256 could fall within a few years of a purpose-built system becoming operational. The Babbush et al. 2026 compilation this relies on is itself very recent, suggesting the circuit-level optimization is still maturing. RSA-2048: The paper’s fastest RSA-2048 attack requires ~102,000 qubits and 97 days, relying on the time-efficient architecture with P = 1,160 parallel Toffoli gates. Even the balanced architecture takes ~27 years. RSA-2048 remains substantially harder than ECC-256 — roughly two orders of magnitude more Toffoli gates 6.5 × 10⁹ vs. 9 × 10⁷ — and this paper doesn’t fundamentally change that ratio. Should cryptographers panic? No. But they should continue migrating to post-quantum standards, and this paper weakens the complacent view that cryptographically relevant Shor implementations are necessarily a distant-2040s issue under all architectures. The theoretical path from demonstrated hardware to cryptographic break has shortened dramatically. Whether the engineering can follow the theory is the open question, and it’s not one that any single paper can answer. The honest assessment: Under the stricter standard of a non-vacuous Shor implementation with genuine quantum contribution, the largest number factored on real hardware remains 15. The most credible path to breaking real cryptography requires sustained operation of tens of thousands of qubits at error rates substantially better than current demonstrations, for days at a time, using codes and surgery protocols that have been designed but not built. That’s a serious path. It’s not a short one. What I Would Want to See Next As someone who has spent this series building tools to evaluate quantum factoring claims, here’s what I’d want to see to increase confidence in these estimates: 1. Large-scale code surgery benchmarks. The paper benchmarks surgery on the smallest processor code \\248, 10, ≤18\\. Benchmarking the larger surgery systems the lp₂₀ processor code and the inter-zone operations would substantially strengthen the resource estimates. The paper acknowledges this as future work. 2. End-to-end compiled circuits. The amortized time-per-Toffoli estimates Extended Data Table V are computed from the dominant subroutines adders and lookups, not from a full circuit compilation. An end-to-end compilation of even a small instance would validate the compilation strategy and time estimates. 3. Experimental demonstration of high-rate codes. The LP codes are elegant in theory. Running even a small instance say, the \\248, 10, ≤18\\ bivariate bicycle code that’s used as a processor/factory code on actual neutral-atom hardware would be a major milestone. 4. Independent reproduction of the code search. The seed matrices are provided, which is excellent. Independent verification of the distance estimates which use randomized algorithms and are upper bounds would be valuable. 5. Publication of the upstream dependencies. Several critical results reference papers “in preparation” — particularly \113\ low-weight logical operator bases for LP codes and \125\ atlas of fault-tolerant quantum memory codes. These do not invalidate the estimates, but they do mean some critical ingredients are not yet independently checkable in full detail. The Bigger Picture I started this series by running Shor’s algorithm on real quantum hardware and finding that 15 was the largest number it could genuinely factor. In Part 2, I showed that most published quantum factoring “records” can’t survive a null-baseline test. In Part 3, I quantified the engineering gap — and found it enormous. This paper represents the most serious theoretical effort to close that gap I’ve seen. The authors are some of the best in the field. The code constructions are novel. The architecture is thoughtful. The analysis is, by the standards of quantum computing resource estimates, unusually transparent about its assumptions and limitations. And yet, the distance between this paper and a working quantum computer that breaks cryptography remains measured in fundamental engineering challenges, not incremental improvements. The codes haven’t been built. The large-scale parallel surgery assumptions underlying the fastest estimates have only limited numerical benchmarking so far. The error rates haven’t been achieved on large systems. The cycle times haven’t been demonstrated. The continuous operation for days hasn’t been attempted. In Attack on Titanhttps://www.imdb.com/title/tt2560140/, the message sent across 2,000 years is a warning and a promise — proof that the future has already happened, that the path is determined, that the struggle matters precisely because its outcome is real. This paper is something similar: a message from a future that the authors can clearly see, built on physics and mathematics that are sound, transmitted through the noise of assumptions and engineering unknowns. The question is not whether 10,000 qubits will eventually suffice — the trajectory of the field makes that increasingly plausible. The question is how many of the assumptions in the stack will survive contact with reality, and how long that contact will take. The paper itself, read honestly, suggests the answer is “most of them, eventually” and “longer than the title implies.” In the meantime, under the standard I’ve applied throughout this series — a non-vacuous Shor implementation with genuine quantum contribution — the largest number a quantum computer has factored remains 15. The gap is narrowing. The future is still arriving one noisy gate at a time. Appendix Key Numbers at a Glance !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/680/1wJuvpeTcodd-dYFwy8Ti1g.png The paper analyzed in this post is: Madelyn Cain, Qian Xu, Robbie King, Lewis R. B. Picard, Harry Levine, Manuel Endres, John Preskill, Hsin-Yuan Huang, Dolev Bluvstein, “Shor’s algorithm is possible with as few as 10,000 reconfigurable atomic qubits,” arXiv:2603.28627v1 \quant-ph\, March 31, 2026.https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.28627v1 !https://medium.com//stat?event=post.clientViewed&referrerSource=fullrss&postId=9ba48f323ecb

title: The Fault in our Qubits
excerpt: What It Would Actually Take to Break RSA with a Quantum Computer
text: What It Would Actually Take to Break RSA with a Quantum Computer !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1dTv69OJVbyQhm5A61NQkXA.png Part 3 of a three-part series on Shor’s algorithm and quantum factoring. Part 1: “Sometimes it’s too Slow…, For Shorhttps://medium.com/@monitsharma/sometimes-its-too-slow-for-shor-c01677032324”, covered our hardware results on IBM Heron processors. Part 2: “The Emperor Has No Factors”https://medium.com/@monitsharma/the-emperor-has-no-factors-9eaec0d9bd0d demonstrated that every published quantum factoring experiment has a null false-positive rate so high that random measurement outcomes would have succeeded. Where We Left Off In Part 1https://medium.com/@monitsharma/sometimes-its-too-slow-for-shor-c01677032324, we ran Shor’s algorithm on IBM’s best available hardware, Heron processors on ibm\torino and ibm\fez , and watched it struggle to factor 15. In Part 2https://medium.com/@monitsharma/the-emperor-has-no-factors-9eaec0d9bd0d, we showed that it doesn't much matter: every published quantum factoring experiment from Vandersypen 2001 through Skosana & Tame 2021 has null false-positive rates so high that the classical post-processing, not the quantum computation, is doing the heavy lifting. Skosana and Tame's factorization of 21 literally cannot fail — all eight possible measurement outcomes yield correct factors under standard continued-fractions recovery. So: the toy experiments don’t work well on real hardware, and even when they do “work,” they aren’t demonstrating what they claim to demonstrate. The natural question is: what would it actually take? Not to factor 15. Not to factor 21. But to factor an RSA-2048 key — the kind of number whose intractability underwrites the security of the internet. This is the question that turns quantum factoring from a physics curiosity into an engineering specification. And the answer, as we’ll see, is sobering. The Scaling Wall Shor’s algorithm is polynomially efficient in theory. Factoring an n\-bit number requires On³ gates in the textbook construction, or On² log n with the optimizations of Gidney and Ekerå 2021https://quantum-journal.org/papers/q-2021-04-15-433/. Polynomial scaling sounds manageable. It is not. The polynomial sits on top of enormous constants, and even polynomial growth becomes punishing when the base input is 2,048 bits and every logical operation must be protected by layers of error correction. Here is what the resource curve looks like when you actually compute it: !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/15Gq7txAnWTdKLQKARHzqYg.png Physical qubits, gate counts, and estimated runtime for factoring numbers of increasing size using optimized Shor’s algorithm with surface code error correction. The dashed red lines mark current hardware capabilities. Note: this is polynomial scaling in the complexity-theoretic sense, but the constants and error-correction overhead make it formidable in practice. The three panels tell the same story from different angles. Current superconducting platforms range from roughly 100 to 1,000 physical qubits, depending on whether one prioritizes performance or raw scale — IBM’s highest-fidelity Heron processors sit at 133–156 qubits, while their largest chip Condor reached 1,121 qubits with reduced per-qubit performance. Factoring an RSA-2048 key requires, by the most careful estimates, somewhere between 100,000 and 20 million physical qubits depending on the error correction architecture assumed more on this shortly. Current circuits decohere after about 100 operations. RSA-2048 demands billions of Toffoli gates. The ratio between where we are and where we need to be is not a gentle slope — it spans multiple orders of magnitude in every dimension. This table makes the scaling concrete. Throughout this post, we use the Gidney-Ekerå 2021 resource model as our primary reference point for consistency, it remains the most widely cited and carefully validated estimate, and its assumptions are transparent. We’ll address more recent and more aggressive estimates below. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1OzlDWJ0JC8bTEruoVK3FqQ.png Estimates from our simplified scaling model optimized Shor’s-style arithmetic, surface code at p = 10⁻³. These are lower bounds: the model counts Toffoli gates and QEC cycle time but does not model magic state factory throughput, lattice surgery routing, or repeated-attempt overhead. For RSA-2048, the full Gidney-Ekerå 2021 analysis — which does account for these factors — gives ~20M physical qubits, ~2.7B Toffoli gates, and ~8 hours of runtime. Our model’s 41.5 minutes and 27.5M qubits differ because it trades a cruder factory model for transparency across the full range of bit sizes. A few things to notice. First, the jump from 4-bit to 2048-bit factoring isn’t a matter of “scaling up” in any normal engineering sense. You need roughly 17,000× more physical qubits, and your gate count goes from single digits to tens of millions. Second, even the 256-bit entry, which would be trivially factorable classically, already demands nearly a million physical qubits. The quantum advantage over classical factoring doesn’t even begin to matter until numbers exceed roughly 800–1000 bits, by which point the quantum machine is a warehouse-scale installation. A Moving Target: Newer Estimates The 20-million-qubit figure from Gidney-Ekerå 2021 is not the last word. Resource estimates have been falling as algorithmic and error-correction techniques improve, a trend worth tracking honestly. In May 2025, Craig Gidney published an updatedhttps://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15917 analysis showing that RSA-2048 could be factored with fewer than one million noisy qubits in under a week, a 20× reduction in qubit count from his 2021 estimate. The reduction comes from three innovations: approximate residue arithmetic that avoids storing full 2048-bit numbers in quantum registers, yoked surface codes that triple the storage density of idle qubits, and magic state cultivation that dramatically reduces the overhead of producing the non-Clifford resource states needed for Toffoli gates. The tradeoff is longer runtime, roughly a week instead of eight hours, but a week is still operationally relevant for an attacker. More recently, in February 2026, Webster et al. proposed the “Pinnacle Architecture”https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11457 using quantum LDPC codes instead of surface codes, arguing that RSA-2048 could be factored with fewer than 100,000 physical qubits and a runtime of about one month. This is another order-of-magnitude reduction, but it relies on QLDPC codes that have not been demonstrated in hardware and require non-local qubit connectivity that current superconducting platforms do not support. These estimates move in one direction — down — and they deserve to be taken seriously. But two things remain constant across all of them. First, every estimate assumes a uniform physical error rate of 10⁻³ sustained across the entire machine for the full duration of the computation. Second, every estimate requires fault-tolerant quantum error correction operating reliably at scale, which no experiment has yet demonstrated. The qubit count is falling; the engineering difficulty is not. Mind the Gap With that context, here is what the gap looks like using the Gidney-Ekerå 2021 reference point: !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1-uF1IEYxnJehCUEzEv0Ow.png Current quantum hardware capabilities blue compared to the requirements for factoring RSA-2048 red, plotted on a logarithmic scale using the Gidney-Ekerå 2021 estimate. “QEC Round Depth” measures sequential error-correction rounds ~3 per Toffoli via lattice surgery, distinct from raw Toffoli count. Under the more recent Gidney 2025 estimate, the qubit gap shrinks from 4.3 to ~2.9 orders of magnitude — still enormous, but meaningfully smaller. The qubit gap against the 2021 estimate is 4.3 orders of magnitude. Against the 2025 estimate, it’s ~2.9 orders of magnitude. Against the as yet theoretical Pinnacle architecture, it’s ~1.9. The QEC depth gap, measuring sequential error-correction rounds, not raw gate count — is 7.9 orders of magnitude. These are not gaps that close with a generation or two of hardware improvement, though the algorithmic progress is clearly working to narrow them. Consider an analogy. In 1903, the Wright brothers flew 120 feet. A Boeing 787 flies 7,600 miles, a factor of about 330,000×, or 5.5 orders of magnitude. That gap was closed in 110 years of sustained aerospace engineering. Even the most aggressive current quantum factoring estimate Pinnacle, ~100K qubits still requires roughly a 100× improvement over the largest current hardware — and that gap must be closed in a fundamentally different technological regime where scaling is constrained by quantum coherence, not just structural engineering. The Error Correction Tax The raw qubit and gate counts are only half the story. Every logical qubit in a fault-tolerant quantum computer is not a single physical qubit, it’s an elaborately encoded structure of many physical qubits, designed to detect and correct errors faster than they accumulate. The leading approach is the surface code, which arranges physical qubits on a 2D grid and uses repeated “syndrome measurements” to catch errors. The code’s error-correcting power is governed by its distance d: a distance-d surface code can correct up to ⌊d-1/2⌋ errors per round. Higher distance means better protection, but also more physical qubits — roughly 2d² per logical qubit. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1EXKEeMbdfKrtidtZKXdqg.png Left: Logical error rate as a function of surface code distance for different physical error rates. Crossing below the RSA-2048 target ~10⁻¹⁵ per round requires distance 17–27 depending on physical error rate. Right: The physical qubit overhead per logical qubit. At distance 27, each logical qubit costs 1,458 physical qubits. Here is the key tension. Current hardware achieves physical error rates around 10⁻³ 0.1% on the best qubit pairs. This is below the surface code threshold ~1%, which means error correction can in principle work. But “in principle” does a lot of heavy lifting in that sentence. At p = 10⁻³, achieving the per-round logical error rate needed for RSA-2048 factoring requires code distance ~27. That’s 1,458 physical qubits per logical qubit — before accounting for magic state distillation factories, routing overhead, and ancilla qubits. The multiplication is unforgiving: 14,532 logical qubits × 1,458 physical/logical × 1.3 factory overhead ≈ 27.5 million physical qubits. And this assumes that the physical error rate holds at 10⁻³ across all those qubits simultaneously. Current hardware can sustain this error rate on individual qubit pairs in carefully calibrated devices of ~100–1000 qubits. Whether it can be sustained across a million-qubit machine — let alone 20 million, is an open and deeply non-trivial engineering question. Error rates tend to degrade as systems scale: crosstalk, frequency collisions, control line interference, and thermal management all get worse with size. The assumption of a uniform 10⁻³ across a large machine is not a physical law. It is an engineering aspiration with no current evidence behind it. Newer approaches like QLDPC codes used in the Pinnacle architecture promise to reduce this overhead dramatically by encoding more logical information per physical qubit. But they introduce their own challenges — notably requiring non-local qubit connectivity that no current superconducting platform provides. When Might We Get There? It’s tempting to extrapolate historical trends and declare a timeline. Let’s do it, with full acknowledgment that such extrapolations are worth approximately what you pay for them. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1i1cFLojO5vIsU4bzYOyF9g.png Left: Historical qubit counts with exponential extrapolation fitted to achieved systems only blue circles. Planned/roadmap systems orange diamond are shown separately. Three target lines correspond to three resource estimates for RSA-2048 factoring. Right: Two-qubit gate error rate trajectory, with rates already approaching the assumed 10⁻³ threshold. The qubit count has been roughly doubling every 1.1 years among achieved systems since 2016. If this trend continues; a large “if”, we’d reach the Gidney 2025 target of one million physical qubits around 2035, or the 2021 target of 20 million around 2040. Error rates have been halving roughly every 1.3 years, with the best reported two-qubit gate errors on select qubit pairs now at or slightly below 10⁻³. But these extrapolations smuggle in assumptions that deserve scrutiny. Qubit count scaling is not just “more of the same.” Going from 1,000 to 1,000,000 qubits isn’t like going from 1 to 1,000 transistors on a chip. Quantum systems face qualitatively different scaling challenges: maintaining coherence across a large system, distributing control signals without introducing crosstalk, managing the classical processing needed for real-time error correction decoding, and physically cooling the entire apparatus to 15 millikelvin. These are not problems that yield to Moore’s Law extrapolation. Error rates must be sustained, not just achieved. The best reported two-qubit error rates come from hand-picked qubit pairs on small devices. The median error rate across a full 1,000-qubit chip is considerably worse. Scaling to millions of qubits while maintaining uniformly low error rates is a materials science, fabrication, and control engineering challenge of a fundamentally different character than achieving low error rates on a few qubits. The timeline assumes no plateaus. Exponential trends in technology famously hit walls, clock speeds plateaued in the mid-2000s, Dennard scaling ended, and many quantum hardware metrics have already shown signs of leveling off at certain technology nodes. Extrapolating the 2016–2023 trend line out by another decade or more assumes uninterrupted exponential improvement, which is historically unusual for any technology. A realistic assessment: the earliest plausible date for a cryptographically relevant quantum factoring demonstration depends heavily on which resource estimate you believe. Under the Gidney 2025 model, if everything goes well, the hardware might exist by the late 2030s. Under the 2021 model, the early 2040s. Under more conservative assumptions about scaling, later still. Whether current superconducting architectures can scale all the way to this regime, sustaining the required error rates across millions of qubits for days of continuous operation, remains an open question. What the Experiments Actually Show Let’s be fair to the experimentalists. Published quantum factoring experiments, for all their limitations as factoring demonstrations, are not scientifically worthless. They serve a different purpose than what their titles claim. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1S53xWOqv6pLIAMbeXBvgkw.png Published factoring experiments blue circles, sized by year plotted against the resource requirements for meaningful factoring targets diamonds and RSA-2048 stars — red for the 2021 estimate, green for 2025. The dashed diagonal line is an illustrative guide, not a precise boundary. The gap between the experimental cluster in the bottom-left and the targets is vast — but the experiments were never really competing on this axis. The cluster of published experiments in the bottom-left corner of this figure lives in a completely different regime from even the most modest useful factoring target. Every published experiment uses fewer than 10 qubits and fewer than 300 gates. The nearest meaningful target 16-bit factoring, which is still trivially classical requires 21,000 physical qubits. But these experiments do demonstrate gate calibration quality, qubit connectivity in specific topologies, control system precision for textbook quantum algorithms, and measurement readout fidelity. These are legitimate hardware characterization milestones. The problem is not the experiments themselves, it’s the framing. When a paper’s title says “Factoring N=21 on a quantum computer,” readers and journalists, and policymakers, and investors understandably interpret this as progress toward breaking cryptography. As we showed in Part 2https://medium.com/@monitsharma/the-emperor-has-no-factors-9eaec0d9bd0d, it is nothing of the sort. A more honest framing would be: “Demonstrating a 5-qubit circuit of depth 20 on superconducting hardware, using the Shor factoring circuit for N=21 as a benchmark.” An Illustrative Scorecard How close are we, really? The following radar chart gives a rough visual summary. A caveat: three of the six axes gate fidelity, connectivity, and error correction are editorial estimates rather than computed ratios, so this figure should be read as an illustration of relative maturity across dimensions, not as a precise measurement. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1D3Ks62qvAcaGfR9t6hO-Q.png Current quantum hardware capabilities as an approximate fraction of RSA-2048 requirements across six dimensions. Axes labeled “log ratio” are computed from log₁₀current/required; axes labeled “estimated” are editorial assessments. Gate fidelity is the closest to target; error correction capability is the furthest. The chart illustrates a pattern of deeply uneven progress. Gate fidelity, the dimension that gets the most attention in press releases, is the closest to where it needs to be. Individual two-qubit gates on the best devices are within an order of magnitude of the Gidney-Ekerå requirement. This is a real achievement. But gate fidelity is the easier part. The dimensions that matter most for practical error-corrected computation, circuit depth, connectivity, coherence time, and above all error correction at scale, lag far behind. And these are the dimensions where progress is hardest, because they involve systems-level engineering challenges rather than individual-component optimization. On error correction specifically: Google’s Willow chip showed below-threshold scaling for a memory-style surface-code experiment, logical error rates decreasing with increasing code distance, which is an important step. But a memory experiment and a computation are very different things. Demonstrating logical error suppression during storage is not the same as maintaining it through a long algorithmic computation with real-time decoding and feed-forward. The gap between “error correction works on a stored state” and “error correction works throughout a multi-billion-gate algorithm” remains large and largely unexplored experimentally. What Would a Meaningful Demonstration Look Like? Given everything we’ve established across this series, what would it take for a quantum factoring experiment to actually mean something? Here are the criteria: 1\. Factor a number that’s too large for the null test to save you. As we showed in Part 2https://medium.com/@monitsharma/the-emperor-has-no-factors-9eaec0d9bd0d, the continued-fractions post-processing pipeline is so forgiving that random measurement outcomes succeed with high probability for small numbers. A meaningful experiment needs to factor a number large enough that the null false-positive rate is negligible, which means using enough precision qubits that random guessing would almost certainly fail. For N=15, you’d need at least t=8 precision qubits to get the null rate below 5%. For larger N, even more. 2\. Factor a number whose factors weren’t used to build the circuit. Every published experiment compiles the modular exponentiation circuit using knowledge of the factors. This is necessary for circuit optimization in the near term, but it means the factors are baked into the hardware before a single qubit is measured. A truly meaningful demonstration would use a general-purpose modular exponentiation circuit, which is exactly the circuit that requires millions of qubits. 3\. Demonstrate that the quantum computation is doing work that a classical null model cannot. Report the null false-positive rate alongside the experimental success rate. Show that the experiment outperforms random guessing through the same post-processing pipeline. This is such a basic scientific control that its absence from two decades of literature is remarkable. 4\. Beat classical factoring. Ultimately, the only meaningful benchmark for quantum factoring is factoring a number that classical algorithms cannot. The current classical factoring record is RSA-250 829 bits, achieved in 2020 using roughly 2,700 CPU-core-yearshttps://phys.org/news/2020-03-cryptographic.html. Any quantum factoring demonstration on a number below ~800 bits is, by definition, slower than a classical computer, so it’s a demonstration of quantum hardware, not quantum advantage. No current or near-term experiment meets any of these criteria. Nor is any expected to within the next decade. What This Means for Cryptography Should we be worried about Shor’s algorithm breaking RSA? The honest answer depends on your time horizon. In the next 10 years 2025–2035: No. Even the most aggressive resource estimates Pinnacle’s ~100K qubits describe hardware that does not exist and requires error-correction architectures that have not been demonstrated. NIST’s ongoing migration to post-quantum cryptographic standards is prudent and well-timed, but it is driven by the “harvest now, decrypt later” threat model, where adversaries collect encrypted data today to decrypt it when quantum computers eventually arrive, not by any imminent capability. In the next 20 years 2035–2045: Possibly, but far from certain. If qubit counts and error rates continue improving at historical rates, and if architectural breakthroughs in error correction close the gap faster than surface code scaling suggests, a demonstration on a number in the hundreds-of-bits range might become feasible. This would be scientifically momentous but not yet cryptographically relevant. The falling resource estimates 20M → <1M → <100K suggest that algorithmic progress may close the gap faster on the qubit-count axis than hardware alone would predict. In the next 30+ years 2045+: Unknown. Predicting technology three decades out is a fool’s errand. It’s possible that entirely different quantum computing architectures topological qubits, photonic systems, new error correction schemes will change the calculus in ways we can’t anticipate. It’s also possible that quantum computing will hit fundamental scaling walls that make fault-tolerant computation at the required scale permanently impractical. The responsible conclusion is: migrate to post-quantum cryptography because it’s cheap insurance, not because the threat is imminent. And be deeply skeptical of anyone claiming quantum computers will break RSA by 2030. They won’t. Conclusions: Honesty as a Service Across three blog posts, I’ve tried to do something simple: be honest about quantum factoring. In Part 1https://medium.com/@monitsharma/sometimes-its-too-slow-for-shor-c01677032324, I showed that Shor’s algorithm on real hardware produces noisy, unreliable results — even for numbers small enough to factor on a pocket calculator. In Part 2https://medium.com/@monitsharma/the-emperor-has-no-factors-9eaec0d9bd0d, I showed that two decades of published “quantum factoring” experiments are undermined by a null hypothesis that nobody checked: classical post-processing succeeds on random input with probability 25–100%, making the quantum computation irrelevant. And in this post, I’ve shown that the gap between these toy experiments and anything cryptographically meaningful spans multiple orders of magnitude in every relevant dimension, even as algorithmic improvements steadily narrow it. None of this means quantum computing is a fraud or a dead end. Quantum hardware has made real, impressive progress on metrics that matter: gate fidelities, qubit counts, coherence times, and initial error correction demonstrations. Headline qubit estimates for quantum factoring have fallen by roughly two orders of magnitude in five years, from 20 million Gidney-Ekerå 2021, surface codes to under 100,000 Pinnacle 2026, QLDPC codes, driven by genuine algorithmic and architectural innovation across increasingly aggressive assumptions. These are legitimate achievements. But they are achievements in understanding how to design a future quantum computer, not achievements in building one that can factor cryptographically relevant numbers. The persistent conflation of “we ran a circuit” with “we factored a number” has done the field no favors. The path from factoring 15 to factoring an RSA key is not a path you walk. It’s a path you build, one breakthrough at a time, and we are very early in the construction. Recognizing this is not pessimism. It’s the kind of clear-eyed engineering assessment that good work requires. The quantum computing community has earned enough real achievements to afford honesty about the ones it hasn’t.
