title: The Emperor Has No Factors
excerpt: What Happens When You Apply Honest Metrics to Every Published Shor’s Result
text: What Happens When You Apply Honest Metrics to Every Published Shor’s Result !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1bhTkK0hjhAauKGPMwv6Wwg.png Introduction: The Two-Qubit Trick In 2013, John Smolin, Graeme Smith, and Alexander Vargo published a short, devastating paper in Nature titled “Oversimplifying quantum factoringhttps://www.nature.com/articles/nature12290”. They built a quantum circuit that “factors” RSA-768; a 232-digit number that had taken teams of researchers coordinating hundred of machines over two years to crack classically. Their circuit used two qubits and one gate. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1W8Cv8jl3Ya9FHgK0hEMgGA.png The circuit for the fully-compiled Shor’s algorithm. The modular exponentiation is the single controlled-NOT, and the quantum Fourier transform is a Hadamard gate. Image taken from \1\. The trick is simple. If the compiler is allowed to know the factors of the number being factored, the entire quantum computation collapses to a trivial verification step. The 2-qubit circuit doesn’t discover the factors, it confirms them, using a structure that was designed with the answers already embedded. Smolin, Smith, and Vargo showed that this reduction applies to any product of unequal primes, regardless of the size. They could “factor” a 20,000-bit number just that easily. This is the RSA-768 number they factored: 1230186684530117755130494958384962720772853569595334792197322 4521517264005072636575187452021997864693899564749427740638459 2519255732630345373154826850791702612214291346167042921431160 2221240479274737794080665351419597459856902143413 = 3347807169895689878604416984821269081770479498371376856891243 388982883793878002287614711652531743087737814467999489 × 3674604366679959042824463379962795263227915816434308764267 6032283815739666511279233373417143396810270092798736308917 Their point was not merely academic. They were responding to a growing body of experimental papers, each one announcing a new quantum factoring “milestone”, that all relied on exactly this type of compiled circuit. In every case, the modular exponentiation oracle, the computationally hard core of Shor’s algorithm, was replaced by a hand-designed shortcut built from prior knowledge of the prime factors. The quantum hardware wasn’t computing anything unknown. It was executing a lookup table. In Part 1/writing/sometimes-its-too-slow-for-shor/ of this series, I ran Shor’s algorithm on IBM’s 156-qubit Heron processor and discovered something uncomfortable: my “successful” factorizations were being recovered by a forging classical post-processing pipeline, not by genuine quantum signal. Even when the quantum circuit output looked like noise, the continued-fractions machinery frequently extracted the correct factors anyway. This post extends that investigation to the published literature. I built a computational framework: the “scorecard engine”, that evaluates the major gate-model Shor experiments from 2001 through 2021 against a standardized null baseline. I also examine the adiabatic/Ising “stunt” factorizations and the controversial Yan et al. lattice-QAOAhttps://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.12372 claim. The results are quantitative, reproducible and in several cases startling. Part 1: Why Null Baselines Matter The Missing Control Experiment Every branch of empirical science has a concept of null hypothesis: what would we observe if the effect we’re testing for were absent? In drug trials, this is the placebo group. In particle physics, it’s the background event rate. In quantum factoring, the natural null hypothesis is: what happens if we replace the quantum computer with a source of uniformly random bits and feed those bits through the same classical post-processing? If random input succeeds at producing the correct factors with high probability, then the experiment has not demonstrated that the quantum hardware contributed anything. The measured “success rate” would need to significantly exceed the null baseline to constitute evidence of quantum computation. Among the major published gate-model Shor experiments I surveyed-Vandersypen 2001https://www.nature.com/articles/414883a, Lu 2007https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.99.250504, Lanyon 2007https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.99.250505, Martin-Lopez 2012https://www.nature.com/articles/nphoton.2012.259, Lucero 2012https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.5707, Monz 2016https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.08852, Amico, Saleem & Kumph 2019https://journals.aps.org/pra/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevA.100.012305, and Skosana & Tame 2021https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-021-95973-w — not a single one reports this comparison. How the Continued Fractions Pipeline Works To understand why the null baseline matters so much for small numbers, let me walk through the classical post-processing step by step. After the quantum phase estimation QPE circuit runs, we measure the t-qubit control register, obtaining an integer y ∈ {0, 1, …, 2^t − 1}. The algorithm then: 1. Computes the phase fraction: φ = y / 2^t. This approximates some rational number s/r, where r is the multiplicative order we seek and s is an unknown integer. 2. Expands as continued fraction: The continued fraction algorithm decomposes φ into a sequence of increasingly precise rational approximations called convergents. For example, 5/8 has convergents 0/1, 1/1, 1/2, 2/3, 5/8. 3. Tests each convergent denominator: For each convergent p/q, the algorithm checks whether q or a small multiple of q is a valid multiplicative order: does a^q ≡ 1 mod N? If so, it attempts factor extraction via gcda^q/2 ± 1, N. 4. Accepts or rejects: If a non-trivial factor emerges, the algorithm succeeds. Otherwise, it tries the next convergent. The critical observation is that with only 2^t possible measurement outcomes and multiple convergents per outcome, the pipeline has many chances to stumble into the correct answer. For t=3, there are only 8 possible y-values. Each one generates 2–5 convergent denominators. If even a few of those denominators happen to coincide with the true order or a multiple of it that still yields factors, the pipeline reports success, regardless of whether the quantum circuit produced those specific y-values with any preference. The Scorecard Engine I built scorecardengine.py to compute this exhaustively. For each published experiment with parameters N,a,t the engine: 1. Enumerates all 2^t possible measurement outcomes. 2. For each outcome y, runs the standard continued fractions pipeline. 3. Checks whether the pipeline produces the correct prime factors. 4. Computes the fraction of outcomes that succeed; the strict null false-positive rate. This is a clean, well-defined quantity: the probability that a uniform random measurement from a t-qubit register yields correct factors through continued fractions post-processing, for a given N,a. No quantum mechanics involved. I also compute a separate adversarial expanded rate that additionally tries adjacent outcomes y ± 1, y ± 2 and multiples of candidate orders. This models an aggressive experimenter scanning beyond the standard pipeline. It is not a faithful reconstruction of any single paper’s published protocol — different papers use different success metrics, and some like Amico et al. bypass continued fractions entirely in favor of statistical overlap measures. The adversarial rate is an upper bound on how forgiving the number-theoretic structure can be. Computing the Ideal QPE Distribution Correctly To compare the null baseline against what a perfect quantum computer would achieve, I need the exact ideal QPE probability distribution. For order r that evenly divides 2^t like r = 4, t = 3, all probability mass concentrates on sharp peaks and the calculation is straightforward. But for r that doesn’t evenly divide 2^t like r = 3, t = 3, which is the case for N = 21 with a = 4, probability mass spreads across multiple outcomes in a characteristic sinc-like pattern. The standard QPE probability of measuring outcome y given eigenvalue phase s/r is: Py|s = sin²π Δ · 2^t / 2^2t · sin²π Δ where Δ = s/r − y/2^t, and Py|s = 1 when Δ is an integer exact peak. The overall probability is then averaged over the r eigenvalue indices: Py = 1/r · Σ\{s=0}^{r−1} Py|s This gives the true per-shot success probability under ideal QPE, correctly handling the spreading that occurs when r does not divide 2^t. The code in scorecardengine.py implements this formula exactly and uses it to weight the factor-extraction check across all outcomes. Part 2: The Results, Experiment by Experiment N=15: The Workhorse The integer 15 = 3 × 5 has been the testing ground for quantum factoring since 2001. It has several properties that make it particularly forgiving for small demonstrations: - With base a = 7, the order is r = 4, which divides 2^t for any t ≥ 2. This means the ideal QPE distribution has perfect peaks with zero leakage. - With base a = 2, the order is also r = 4. - With base a = 11, the order is r = 2 — the smallest possible non-trivial order, which makes factor extraction almost automatic. - N = 15 has only two non-trivial factors, and they’re both small single-digit primes. These properties conspire to make N = 15 extraordinarily vulnerable to false positives. Vandersypen et al. 2001 — The Original The first experimental demonstration used a 7-qubit liquid-state NMR system. The control register had t = 3 qubits 8 possible outcomes with base a = 7. Null baseline analysis: Of the 8 possible uniformly random outcomes, 6 yield correct factors through the continued-fractions pipeline. The strict null FP rate is 75%. A random number generator would “factor” 15 three-quarters of the time. Why is it so high? Because with r = 4 and t = 3, the convergent denominators from most outcomes include 4 or a divisor of 4 namely 2, and gcd7² ± 1, 15 = gcd48, 15 or gcd50, 15 gives factors in either case. Only outcomes y = 0 and y = 4 fail — the former trivially measuring zero gives no information and the latter because its only convergent denominators are 1 and 2, and r = 2 yields a^r/2 = 7 ≡ 7 mod 15, where gcd6, 15 = 3 and gcd8, 15 = 1… actually that does work. Let me be precise: under the generalized factor extraction in my pipeline which tries gcda^k − 1, N for divisors of r, 6 of 8 succeed. The ideal QPE success rate is 50.0%. This means the ideal quantum distribution is actually worse than random at producing factors, because the quantum peaks concentrate probability on outcomes that don’t always include order-4 convergents, while the broad random distribution happens to hit more factor-yielding outcomes. This is a genuinely surprising result that illustrates how a forgiving post-processing pipeline can invert our intuitions about signal quality. This does not mean the Vandersypen experiment was scientifically worthless. It was a landmark demonstration that seven nuclear spins could be coherently manipulated to execute an algorithm. But as a demonstration of factoring — of discovering unknown information — it is indistinguishable from a well-crafted random number generator. Lu et al. 2007 and Lanyon et al. 2007 — Photonic Compilations Both experiments used 4-photon systems with t = 2 qubits in the control register, using base a = 2. With only 4 possible outcomes, the null baseline is brutally high: 50%. A coin flip. The ideal QPE rate is also 50%. There is mathematically no way to distinguish quantum signal from random noise at this resolution. Martin-Lopez et al. 2012 — Qubit Recycling This experiment introduced an architecturally important innovation: the semiclassical QFT with qubit recycling, which reduces the control register to a single physical qubit that is measured and reused iteratively. This technique, based on Kitaev’s iterative phase estimation, is genuinely important for scaling. But the factoring result itself — N = 15, a = 2, effective t = 3 — has the same 75% null FP rate as Vandersypen. Monz et al. 2016 — Trapped Ions, “Scalable” The Innsbruck trapped-ion team used 5 qubits with t = 4 in the control register and base a = 2. With 16 possible outcomes, the null baseline drops to 37.5% — better than earlier experiments, but still alarmingly high. The ideal QPE rate is 50.0%. The paper’s claim of “scalable” architecture referring to the in-sequence measurement capability is architecturally defensible — the hardware could in principle be extended to longer iterative sequences. But the factoring result remains firmly in the high-false-positive regime. Amico, Saleem & Kumph 2019 — The N = 35 Attempt This paper is critically important for our analysis because it studied three numbers 15, 21, and 35 on IBM’s ibmqx5 16-qubit processor, using split-circuit iterative execution with the semiclassical QFT. Notably, Amico et al. used the square of the statistical overlap SSO as their success metric rather than continued-fraction-based factor recovery, so the “same pipeline” framing doesn’t apply literally to their work. For N = 15 with a = 11: The order is r = 2, which makes the continued-fractions pipeline almost trivially successful. The null FP rate is 87.5% — seven of eight random outcomes yield correct factors. For N = 21 with a = 4: Same as other N = 21 experiments — 25% null FP. For N = 35 with a = 4: This is where things get interesting. The order of 4 mod 35 is r = 6. With t = 3 qubits giving only 8 possible outcomes, the continued-fractions pipeline cannot extract r = 6 from any single outcome under my standardized post-processing test. The strict null FP rate is 0.0%. This does not mean that every conceivable classical recovery strategy would fail on these 8 outcomes — only that the standard Shor-style continued-fractions pipeline, as implemented in my scorecard engine, finds no path from any y ∈ {0,…,7} to the correct factors of 35. The problem is that 6 doesn’t divide 8, so the ideal QPE peaks don’t land on integer positions, and with only 3 bits of phase resolution, the continued fractions can’t resolve s/6 accurately enough. Amico et al. reported that the N = 35 experiment largely failed, with roughly 14% success where success is measured by their SSO metric. The high cumulative gate errors from the deep N = 35 circuits overwhelmed the quantum signal. This is the most informative data point in the entire survey: it shows where compiled Shor hits the wall on real hardware, and the 0% null FP rate under the standard pipeline means that any genuine success at this point would be attributable to quantum computation. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1iwPzjGW0EbOKBE0xKeTG2w.png N = 21: The Current Frontier Lucero et al. 2012 — First N = 21 on Superconducting Hardware Using a Josephson phase qubit processor with about 11 CX gates in the compiled circuit, this was the first factorization of 21 on superconducting hardware. The null baseline analysis gives 25% strict FP rate. Skosana & Tame 2021 — The Most Rigorous N = 21 Demonstration This paper deserves detailed attention because it is, to my knowledge, the most carefully characterized compiled Shor demonstration published to date. Skosana and Tame used a 5-qubit circuit 3 control, 2 work on IBM’s ibmq\casablanca 7Q and ibmq\toronto 27Q processors. The key innovation was replacing standard Toffoli gates with Margolus gates relative-phase Toffoli gates, which halve the CX count per Toffoli from 6 to 3. This brought the total circuit down to 25 CX gates with circuit depth 35. Their characterization was rigorous: - Kolmogorov distance from ideal: 0.169 toronto and 0.178 casablanca, compared to 0.435 for uniform noise. - State fidelity via tomography: ~0.70 on both processors. - Entanglement verification: A projector-based witness confirmed non-separability between control and work registers across most bipartitions. These metrics genuinely demonstrate that the hardware is operating coherently in the quantum regime. The Kolmogorov distance in particular shows the output distribution is far from uniform noise and close to the ideal. This is real physics. But the factoring claim itself? The null baseline is 25% strict FP. The ideal QPE success rate, correctly computed from the exact probability distribution, is 47.1%. The quantum signal is roughly 22 percentage points above the null baseline — meaningful but modest, and critically, never reported as a comparison in the paper. No reviewer asked for it. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1PPsis8a-QEn8zjRRNHoag.png Here is the outcome-by-outcome breakdown: !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1KnHkgpZ36DaeeYj1jwKp8w.png Outcomes 3 and 5 are the only successes. Their continued fraction expansions happen to produce 3 as a convergent denominator, which is the true order. Since a = 4 is a perfect square 4 = ²², factor extraction works despite r = 3 being odd: we compute √a^r = ²³ = 8, then gcd8 − 1, 21 = 7 and gcd8 + 1, 21 = 3. The ideal QPE distribution places about 35% probability on y = 0 a failure mode, since it gives no phase information, and roughly 25% each on y = 3 and y = 5 the successful outcomes. This is why the ideal success rate is 47.1%, not 50% — the y = 0 peak wastes significant probability. The Comprehensive Scorecard The table below shows three null baselines at increasing levels of post-processing generosity, plus the ideal QPE success rate for comparison. The “textbook” column uses pure Shor: continued fractions only, even-r required, standard gcd extraction. The “liberal” column adds the perfect-square-base rescue used by Skosana & Tame for a = 4, r = 3, divisor scanning, and multiples of candidate orders. Both are computed by exhaustive enumeration over all 2^t outcomes. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1Kux6RukxfrGnCSqlO-gK1w.png A Methodological Surprise: What the Dual Baseline Reveals The most interesting finding in this table is the gap between textbook and liberal rates for N = 21. Under pure textbook Shor, the null FP rate for N = 21 with a = 4 is 0%. The reason: the true order r = 3 is odd, and textbook Shor’s algorithm says “if r is odd, discard this base and restart with a new random choice of a.” No outcome from a 3-bit register can produce a correct even-order candidate through continued fractions alone, because the true order is odd and no false even order happens to work. The 25% liberal rate exists entirely because of the perfect-square-base rescue strategy. Since a = 4 = 2², we can compute √a^r = 2³= 8 even though r = 3 is odd. Then gcd8 ± 1, 21 gives the factors. This is the strategy Skosana & Tame explicitly use — and it’s a legitimate mathematical technique — but it goes beyond the textbook algorithm. This creates a subtle interpretive question: which null baseline is the right comparison? The answer depends on what claim you’re evaluating: - If the claim is “Shor’s algorithm as described in Nielsen & Chuang successfully factors 21,” then the textbook baseline 0% is the right comparison, and the 47.1% ideal success rate represents a substantial quantum signal. - If the claim is “our post-processing pipeline recovers factors from the quantum output,” then the liberal baseline 25% is the right comparison, because the pipeline does use the perfect-square trick. The 47.1% ideal rate is still above 25%, but the margin is narrower. Neither framing makes the experiment invalid. But the gap between 0% and 25% illustrates why precise methodology labeling matters. The qualitative conclusion — that there is genuine quantum signal for N = 21 above the appropriate null baseline — holds under both framings. The quantitative margin differs substantially. For N = 15, the textbook rates are lower than the liberal rates but still high: 25–50% depending on the base and t. The qualitative conclusion there is unaffected — these are high false-positive rates under either definition. Part 3: The Compilation Problem What “Compiled” Actually Means In standard software engineering, a compiler translates human-readable code into machine-executable instructions without altering the program’s logic. The compiler does not need to know the program’s output to produce correct machine code. In experimental quantum factoring, “compilation” means something categorically different. The circuit designer knows the prime factors of N in advance and uses that knowledge to construct a dramatically simplified modular exponentiation oracle. Rather than building a general-purpose circuit that computes a^x mod N for arbitrary x in superposition, the compiled circuit hardcodes the specific cyclic permutation structure of a^x mod N for the known a, N pair. For N = 21 with a = 4: - The full modular exponentiation sequence is 4^x mod 21 for x = 0, 1, 2, …, which cycles through {1, 4, 16, 1, 4, 16, …} with period 3. - A compiled circuit only needs to implement the 3-element cyclic permutation {1 → 4 → 16 → 1} in the work register, controlled by the counting register. - Skosana & Tame encode these three states in a 2-qubit work register as |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩ a log-compression of the full 5-qubit register that would be needed to represent integers up to 21. The resulting 25 CX-gate circuit is a remarkable piece of engineering. But it is engineering the answer into the question. Craig Gidneyhttps://x.com/CraigGidney has estimated that a general-purpose, uncompiled circuit for N = 21 would require approximately 2,405 two-qubit gates this is a CX-equivalent estimate from circuit synthesis, not an experimentally measured count; the exact number depends on the compilation strategy used. The ~96× gap between 25 and 2,405 represents work done by the classical compiler, not the quantum processor. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1r4qYpG09WxfhxIBh0wTHA.png The Smolin-Smith-Vargo Argument in Detail Smolin, Smith, and Vargo’s 2013 Nature paper formalized this critique. Their key contribution was proving that for any composite N = pq with p ≠ q, there exists a base a with order r = 2. For such a base, the QPE circuit reduces to a single controlled-NOT, and the factor extraction is automatic: a^r/2 = a, and gcda ± 1, N gives the factors. To find such a base, one needs to know the factors — which is precisely the information the algorithm is supposed to discover. But in a compiled experiment, the factors are already known. So the experimenter can always choose the easiest possible base, build the smallest possible circuit, and report “success.” Smolin et al. demonstrated this by providing explicit circuits to “factor” RSA-768 and a synthetic 20,000-bit number, each using only 2 qubits. Their paper concluded that the correct measure of difficulty in Shor’s algorithm is not the size of the number factored, but the length of the period found and the precision of the phase estimation. The Gate Count Reality The gap between compiled and uncompiled circuits is enormous and grows rapidly: !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1SvsNQMFK4Qc4mUqmxauXwQ.png !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/195UEOaVFzs-A7Oc7HKPFA.png For N = 51, Geller and Zhou’s theoretical circuits use only 4 CNOT gates because 51 = 3 × 17 is a product of Fermat primeshttps://mathworld.wolfram.com/FermatPrime.html, which guarantees all multiplicative orders are powers of 2. This is the most extreme case of structural exploitation in the literature. Their paper has never been experimentally realized. Current NISQ hardware can reliably execute circuits with roughly 50–100 two-qubit gates before noise overwhelms the signal this threshold varies by platform and is improving. Compiled circuits for N = 15 and N = 21 fall comfortably within this budget. Uncompiled circuits for even N = 21 exceed it by an order of magnitude. This is why no genuine, uncompiled factoring has been demonstrated on quantum hardware — not because the algorithms are wrong, but because the circuits are too deep for current noise levels Part 4: The Taxonomy of Non-Shor Claims Category B: Adiabatic/Ising Factorizations Parallel to the gate-model Shor experiments, a completely different approach to quantum factoring emerged: reformulating the problem as an Ising energy minimization suitable for adiabatic quantum annealers. This approach does not use Shor’s algorithm at all — no QPE, no QFT, no modular exponentiation. Instead, the binary multiplication table p × q = N is encoded as a quadratic pseudo-Boolean function, and the quantum device searches for the ground state of the corresponding Hamiltonian. The critical issue is that classical preprocessing can eliminate most of the binary variables before the quantum device is even involved. For any odd semiprime N = p × q, we know immediately that both p and q are odd LSBs = 1 and that their most significant bits are 1. Further constraints cascade through the multiplication table, progressively fixing variables. When the prime factors are close together — specifically, when |p − q| is small relative to √N — the classical preprocessing eliminates almost everything, leaving the quantum device with zero to two effective free variables. N = 143 = 11 × 13 Xu et al. 2012https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.108.130501, 4-qubit NMR The factors differ by only 2 and have identical bit-lengths 4 bits each. Fermat’s classical method factors 143 in exactly one step: ⌈√143⌉ = 12, and 12² − 143 = 1 = 1², giving p = 12 + 1 = 13 and q = 12 − 1 = 11. The “quantum” computation had effectively ~1 free variable to solve. N = 56,153 = 233 × 241 Dattani & Bryans 2014https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.6758, theoretical/4-qubit Dattani and Bryans made a crucial mathematical observation: the reduced Ising Hamiltonian for 56,153 has the same structure as the one for 143. Their paper provides the formal proof of this equivalence. My analysis code verifies the consequence — that 56,153 is equally trivially factorable by Fermat’s method 1 step — but does not independently reproduce the Hamiltonian equivalence proof. Fermat’s method: ⌈√56153⌉ = 237, and 237² − 56153 = 16 = 4², giving p = 237 + 4 = 241 and q = 237 − 4 = 233. N = 4,088,459 = 2,017 × 2,027 Dash et al.https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.10478 2018, 2-qubit IBM Q Twin-prime-like proximity. Fermat’s method: 1 step. N = 1,099,551,473,989 = 1,048,589 × 1,048,601 Q2B Conference 2019https://www.newscientist.com/article/2227387-quantum-computer-sets-new-record-for-finding-prime-number-factors/, 3 qubits The factors differ by only 12 across a trillion-scale number. Fermat’s method: 1 step. The pattern is unmistakable: as the “record” N grows exponentially, the qubit count stays constant or decreases, and Fermat’s classical method always factors the number in a single step. The claimed numbers get bigger, but the actual computational difficulty doesn’t change. Each of these numbers was specifically chosen or found to have factors that are absurdly close together, making the classical preprocessing eliminate all of the hard work. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/11eCi02GGp37ZkiUjOpWJYQ.png A modern laptop running Fermat’s method can factor all of these “record-breaking” numbers in microseconds. Category C: The Yan et al. Lattice-QAOA Controversy In late 2022, a team led by Bao Yan published a paperhttps://arxiv.org/abs/2212.12372 claiming to factor a 48-bit number 261,980,999,226,229 = 15,538,213 × 16,860,433 using only 10 qubits on a superconducting processor. The approach combined Schnorr’s classical lattice-based factoring method with the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm QAOA to solve a specific sub-problem. The alarm came from the paper’s scaling claim: under their theoretical model, a 2048-bit RSA key could be broken with merely a few hundred qubits. This directly contradicted the established consensus based on Gidney and Ekerå’s 2021https://quantum-journal.org/papers/q-2021-04-15-433/ analysis that roughly 20 million noisy physical qubits would be needed. The cryptographic community identified the fatal flaw quickly: Schnorr’s classical algorithm itself requires lattice dimensions that grow exponentially with the target integer’s bit length. The quantum QAOA subroutine operates within the lattice framework and cannot bypass this classical scaling barrier. The 48-bit factorization succeeded because the lattice dimension for a 48-bit number is tiny — not because the algorithm had found a shortcut around the fundamental complexity. The consensus among cryptographers is that the lattice-QAOA approach does not constitute a near-term or long-term threat to RSA. The quantum component provides modest optimization within a framework whose classical foundation collapses at scale Part 5: Geller and Zhou’s Theoretical Circuits for N = 51 and N = 85 The 2013 paper by Geller and Zhouhttps://arxiv.org/abs/1304.0128 deserves separate attention because it illustrates the extreme end of structural exploitation The integers 51 = 3 × 17 and 85 = 5 × 17 are products of Fermat primes primes of the form 2^2^k + 1. This guarantees that the multiplicative order of any coprime base a mod N is a power of 2. When all orders are powers of 2, the QPE peaks land on exact integer positions in the measurement register, eliminating the rounding error that plagues non-power-of-2 orders. The compressed modular exponentiation circuits for these numbers require at most 4 CNOT gates no Toffoli gates needed, because the modular exponentiation reduces to a simple bit-copy operation after compression. The total circuit uses 8 qubits: 4 in each register. My null baseline analysis for representative bases: !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1AazJgdAy7tv6uYKygkaz9g.png Even with 16 possible outcomes t = 4, most base choices yield null FP rates above 25%. Only the r = 4 cases drop below 20%. Geller and Zhou acknowledged honestly in their paper that they “do not regard the factorization of products of Fermat primes to be genuine implementations of Shor’s algorithm.” They viewed their circuits as “quasi-legitimate implementations of quantum order finding” — a more careful framing than many other papers in the field. Part 6: What Would Genuine Progress Look Like? After this survey, I want to be constructive. The field is not stuck — hardware is genuinely improving. But the reporting standards need to catch up with the hardware. Here is a concrete checklist that a credible future factoring result should satisfy: Minimum Reporting Requirements 1. Null baseline comparison. Compute and report the strict null FP rate for the exact N, a, t parameters used. Compare the observed per-shot factor yield against this baseline with appropriate statistical testing. This is the single most important missing metric in the entire field. 2. Raw measurement histogram with ideal overlay. Show the complete distribution of measurement outcomes alongside the theoretical ideal. Let readers visually assess signal quality. Skosana & Tame did this well; most earlier papers did not. 3. Per-shot factor yield. Report what fraction of individual measurements, when fed through the post-processing pipeline, produce correct factors. Do not report only “the correct factors were obtained” without shot-level statistics. 4. Peak enrichment metric. Compute the ratio of measured probability mass within ±1 of ideal peak locations to the uniform expectation. This quantifies how much the quantum device concentrates probability where it should, independent of whether those peaks happen to yield factors. 5. Multiple coprime bases. Run the algorithm with several randomly selected bases and report aggregate statistics. A single lucky base choice can produce misleading results, especially for small N where some bases have trivially small orders. 6. Honest gate count disclosure. Report both the compiled circuit’s gate count and an estimate of what the uncompiled circuit would require, with a source for the estimate. This makes transparent how much computational work the classical compiler is performing. 7. Separation of quantum signal from post-processing artifacts. Demonstrate that the factor-extraction success rate significantly exceeds what a random input source would achieve through the same pipeline. For N = 21 with t = 3, this means showing per-shot success significantly above 25%, with enough shots for statistical confidence. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1Tb1OUqaj8Vj4EPIVGTgXiA.png The N = 35 Frontier The Amico et al. N = 35 result is the clearest signpost for where to aim. Under the standard Shor-style pipeline with t = 3, no random outcome produces correct factors 0% null FP. The problem is genuinely hard at this resolution. Any compiled experiment that reliably factors 35 with clear evidence of factor recovery exceeding the null baseline would represent meaningful progress beyond N = 21. Better still: an experiment using a number whose factors were chosen by someone other than the circuit designer — a truly blind trial — would constitute an even stronger demonstration, though this requires uncompiled circuits that are currently too deep for hardware. The Long Road to Cryptographic Relevance For context on where the field stands relative to practical significance: Gidney and Ekerå 2021 estimate that factoring a 2048-bit RSA key with Shor’s algorithm would require approximately 20 million noisy physical qubits running for about 8 hours, using surface code error correction. In a remarkable follow-up published in May 2025, Gidney alone reduced this estimate to under a million noisy qubitshttps://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15917, though the runtime increased to roughly a week. In a more recent paper by Webster et.al. , they further reduced the estimate to 100,000 physical qubitshttps://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11457. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1hOr-AV317o5f3ysoiJHwpQ.png Current hardware has roughly 1,000 noisy qubits with error rates orders of magnitude too high for the required error correction overhead. The gap between “factor 35” and “factor a 2048-bit key” is not a matter of incremental improvement — it requires breakthroughs in physical qubit quality, error correction scaling, and classical control systems operating at microsecond latency across millions of qubits. Part 7: What the Experiments Do Demonstrate I want to be clear about what I am and am not arguing. I am not claiming these experiments are scientifically worthless, nor that the researchers were dishonest. Every one of these papers advanced our understanding of quantum hardware in important ways: - Vandersypen 2001 proved that coherent multi-qubit manipulation was physically possible. - Martin-Lopez 2012 demonstrated qubit recycling, a technique essential for future scaling. - Monz 2016 showed that trapped-ion hardware could perform in-sequence measurements with feed-forward. - Skosana & Tame 2021 demonstrated that approximate Toffoli gates could reduce circuit depth while preserving functional correctness, and their entanglement verification is the most thorough in the literature. - Amico et al. 2019 pushed to N = 35 and honestly reported the failure, providing the most informative negative result in the field. These are genuine hardware milestones. They demonstrate improving gate fidelities, growing qubit counts, novel error-mitigation techniques, and increasingly sophisticated classical-quantum integration. What they do not demonstrate is quantum factoring in the sense of discovering unknown information through quantum speedup. The distinction matters because conflating hardware characterization with computational capability leads to confused public understanding. When a press release says “quantum computer factors 21,” a reasonable reader imagines a machine that was given 21 and returned 3 × 7 without knowing the answer in advance. That is not what happened. What happened is that a team of physicists designed a circuit from the answer 3 × 7, ran it on noisy hardware, and showed the hardware was operating coherently enough to approximately reproduce the designed output. Both narratives are scientifically valuable. But they answer different questions, and pretending they answer the same question is how the field’s credibility erodes. Conclusion Among the compiled gate-model hardware demonstrations with clear factor recovery that I surveyed, N = 21 remains the strongest successful case. Amico et al. 2019 also attempted N = 35, but with poor success ~14% due to cumulative gate errors. The “record-breaking” large numbers in the Ising/adiabatic category 143 through 1.1 trillion don’t use Shor’s algorithm and are trivially factorable by Fermat’s classical method. The null baseline analysis reveals a systematic gap in the literature’s reporting. For most N = 15 experiments, random noise succeeds at producing correct factors 50–87% of the time under a standardized Shor-style post-processing test. For N = 21, the null rate is 25% against an ideal QPE rate of 47.1% — quantum signal exists but has never been compared to the baseline. For N = 35 with t = 3, the null rate drops to 0% under the standard pipeline — the problem is genuinely hard at that resolution, which is exactly where hardware failed. The honest framing is what lets us recognize genuine progress. The N = 35 case points the way: when someone demonstrates reliable factor recovery for a problem where the null baseline is near zero, using a circuit that doesn’t embed the answer, we’ll know the field has turned a corner. The metrics to recognize that moment now exist. The experiments that demonstrate it do not yet. All code for the scorecard engine, figure generation, and Ising tractability analysis is available in the accompanying repository. Every number in this post is reproducible from the scripts. Part 1/writing/sometimes-its-too-slow-for-shor/ covered my own implementation on IBM’s 156-qubit Heron processor. Part 3 will explore what modifications to the algorithm and post-processing could genuinely demonstrate quantum advantage in period finding. The rate is the fraction of y-values that succeed. The “adversarial expanded” rate additionally tries y ± 1, y ± 2, and multiples of candidate orders. title: Sometimes It’s Too Slow… for Shor!!
excerpt: Factoring Numbers on a 133/156-Qubit Quantum Computer: A Deep Dive into Shor’s Algorithm on Quantum Hardware
text: Factoring Numbers on a 133/156-Qubit Quantum Computer: A Deep Dive into Shor’s Algorithm on Quantum Hardware A comprehensive guide to implementing Shor’s factoring algorithm on IBM’s latest quantum hardware — covering the theory, the engineering decisions, the code, and the honest limits of what’s actually possible today. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1boBydVXa2LefrnxglEIRig.jpeg Introduction In 1994, mathematician Peter Shor published what would become one of the most consequential algorithms in computer science: a method for factoring integers in polynomial time on a quantum computer. The implications were staggering — RSA encryption, the backbone of internet security, relies on the assumption that factoring large numbers is computationally intractable. Shor’s algorithm showed that this assumption holds only so long as large-scale quantum computers don’t exist. Three decades later, IBM’s 156-qubit Heron processors represent the cutting edge of publicly accessible quantum hardware. I set out to write a complete, working implementation of Shor’s algorithm targeting these machines, and to answer a deceptively simple question: what is the biggest number a 156-qubit quantum computer can actually factor? The answer, as we’ll see, involves a tension between theoretical qubit capacity and the brutal realities of quantum noise. This post walks through every step: how Shor’s algorithm works, the engineering decisions behind the code, what the academic literature says about the state of the art, and where the limits really are. How Shor’s Algorithm Works Shor’s algorithm elegantly reduces the problem of integer factoring to a problem quantum computers are naturally good at: finding the period of a function. The Classical Reduction Given a composite odd number N that the we want to factor, the algorithm proceeds as follows: 1. Pick a random integer a where 1 < a < N. 2. Compute gcda,N using the classical Euclidean algorithm. If the result is greater than 1, you’ve found a factor lucky shortcut. 3. Find the order r, the smallest positive integer such that a^r ≡ 1mod N. This is the hard step classically, but efficient on a quantum computer. 4. If r is even, and a^r/2 !≡ -1mod N, then at least one of gcda^r/2 -1 , N and gcda^r/2 + 1, N will be a non-trivial factor of N with high probability. The hard part classically is finding the order r. Shor’s quantum speedup comes from the fact that order finding can be reformulated as a phase estimation problem for the modular multiplication unitary. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1ervQTu1LeNtvChTDBWmKw.png Quantum Phase Estimation extracts a phase related to r, and classical post-processing recovers the order. The Quantum Part: Phase Estimation The quantum part of Shor’s algorithm uses phase estimation to solve the order-finding problem. For a chosen integer a coprime to N, define the unitary operator !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1UX2A0s4MC6f-DqIUN9bVA.png Because multiplication by a mod N permutes the integers modulo N, this transformation is reversible and therefore unitary. The key fact is that the eigenvalues of U\a​ are of the form !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/123rPY08oV0iPxlm11DNMw.png where r is the order of amod N and s∈{0,1,…,r−1}. Shor’s algorithm uses Quantum Phase Estimation QPE to estimate one of these phases: - A counting register is prepared in an equal superposition using Hadamard gates. - A work register is initialized to ∣1⟩, which can be expressed as a superposition of eigenstates of U\a​. - Controlled powers U\a^{2k}​ are applied, which imprint phase information onto the counting register. - The inverse Quantum Fourier Transform is applied to the counting register. - Measuring the counting register gives an integer m, such that the ratio !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1S64JO-KLg5fWEwVQOyEFA.png is a good approximation to !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1u4pOtfo-6KDNzR-SqtczDw.png A classical continued fractions procedure is then used to recover a candidate denominator from this approximation. If the recovered value does not yield the correct order, the algorithm is repeated. At a high level, this gives Shor’s algorithm polynomial-time complexity in the number of bits of N, in dramatic contrast to the best known classical factoring algorithms, such as the General Number Field Sieve, which run in sub-exponential time. Why It Matters for Cryptography RSA encryption typically uses 2048-bit or 4096-bit keys. Gidney and Ekerahttps://quantum-journal.org/papers/q-2021-04-15-433/ estimated in 2021 that factoring a 2048-bit RSA integer would require approximately 20 million noisy qubits running for about 8 hours. In a remarkable follow-up published in May 2025, Gidney alone reduced this estimate to under a million noisy qubitshttps://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15917, though the runtime increased to roughly a week. In a more recent paper by Webster et.al. , they further reduced the estimate to 100,000 physical qubitshttps://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11457. We are still orders of magnitude away from this capability. IBM’s entire deployed fleet of quantum systems totals well under 10,000 qubits but the trajectory of improvement is what motivates the ongoing transition to post-quantum cryptography. !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/13updJiRNwwafF7c6FQF22w.png The Hardware IBM’s 133-Qubit Heron r1 For the N=15 and N=21 experiments, I ran the circuits on ibm\torino, a system built on IBM’s 133-qubit Heron r1 processor. On paper, that sounds almost absurdly powerful for a toy factoring experiment. Shor’s algorithm for 15 is supposed to be the baby example — the kind of thing people use to explain the algorithm, not stress-test one of IBM’s best machines. But that is exactly the point. In real hardware, the problem is not whether the device has enough qubits. The problem is whether it can survive the depth, routing, and two-qubit error accumulation created by modular arithmetic once the circuit is transpiled to actual hardware connectivity. That is where Heron matters. IBM introduced Heron r1 in late 2023 as the first processor in its new Heron family: 133 fixed-frequency superconducting qubits connected with tunable couplers. IBM presented it as a major step beyond the earlier Eagle generation, emphasizing better overall performance, lower cross-talk, and a shift away from the old race of “just add more qubits.” In other words, Heron was built to improve the quality of quantum computation, not just the headline qubit count. And for a Shor experiment, that is exactly the hardware regime you want to probe. Factoring circuits are nasty little monsters. They are not impressed by marketing numbers. They care about whether controlled modular multiplication can be compiled into a circuit that still has some coherent signal left by the time measurement happens. A processor can have more than a hundred qubits and still fail miserably if the transpiled circuit becomes too deep or if the two-qubit gates are not clean enough. Heron r1 is interesting precisely because it pushes that boundary farther than earlier superconducting chips, but not nearly far enough to make textbook period-finding easy. IBM’s public system listings identify ibm\torino as a 133-qubit Heron r1 machine, with platform-level throughput metrics like CLOPS reported around 290K. That makes it one of the most capable public superconducting systems available for this kind of experiment. But even here, the basic lesson is brutal: having a state-of-the-art chip does not magically make Shor practical. It just lets you see the limits more clearly. That is why this hardware matters in the story. Heron r1 is not a weak device. It is one of the strongest public devices available. If even this machine struggles to produce clean period-finding structure for tiny composites, then the bottleneck is not hype, not bad luck, and not sloppy implementation. The bottleneck is the current reality of quantum hardware itself. IBM’s 156-Qubit Heron Processor The IBM Quantum Heron processor, first unveiled at the IBM Quantum Summit in December 2023, is IBM’s highest-performance quantum processor, available to the public. The original version r1 featured 133 qubits. In November 2024, IBM released the Heron r2 with 156 qubits in a heavy-hexagonal lattice topology with tunable couplers. Key Specifications The Heron r2 achieves a median two-qubit CZ gate error rate of approximately 3 × 10⁻³, which is roughly 10 times better than the previous generation 127-qubit Eagle processors. Its speed, measured in Circuit Layers Operations Per Second CLOPS reached 250,000, another 10x improvement. IBM has states that the Heron r2 can reliably execute quantum circuits with up to 5,000 two-qubit gate operations. The 133-qubit Heron r1 is available through ibmtorino. In July 2025, IBM released the Heron r3 revision with further manufacturing improvements impacting coherence, gate fidelity, and readout performance. The Qubit Budget: How Big a Number Can We Factor? This is where theory meets reality, and where most online discussions of Shor’s algorithm on real hardware get it wrong. Theoretical Maximum Qubit Count Only There are three main circuit architectures for Shor’s algorithm, each with a different qubit requirements for factoring an n\-bit number N: !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1K3zLp6fENdhdpOHW03H19w.png The Beauregard Circuit is the standard reference, published in 2002https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0205095. It performs all modular arithmetic in Fourier space, using phase rotations instead of explicit binary adders, achieving the factoring of an n-bit integer with only 2n+3 qubits. This means 156 qubits could theoretically handle numbers up to 76 bits ,roughly 7.5 ×10 ²². The iterative QPE approach also called the semiclassical QFT uses Kitaev’s technique of recycling a single controlled qubit with mid circuit measurement and classical feed-forward, reducing the requirement to just n+1 qubits. This would push the theoretic limit to 155-bit numbers on 156 qubits. However, it requires dynamic circuits with classical control flow, which adds complexity in real hardware. The Real Bottleneck: Circuit Depth Qubit count is only half the story. The other critical constraint is circuit depth — specifically, the number of two-qubit gates the circuit requires. Every two-qubit gate introduces error, and errors compound multiplicatively. On the IBM Heron r2 processor, with a median CZ gate error rate of approximately 0.3%, the probability that an entire circuit executes without any gate error is roughly 0.997^g, where g is the total two-qubit gate count. This survival probability collapses exponentially. The Heron r2 can reliably execute circuits with up to roughly 5,000 two-qubit gates. Beyond that threshold, noise overwhelms the signal and the hardware output becomes indistinguishable from uniform random noise. Here is what that means in practice. The table below shows the measured and extrapolated two-qubit gate counts for factoring semiprimes of increasing size using the standard textbook QPE approach with precomputed permutation oracles: !https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1GZldfPqyAXDER2g7kaR9hw.png The gate counts for N = 15, 21, and 35 are measured from actual hardware submissions after transpilation to the ISA gate set. The estimates for larger N are extrapolated from the observed scaling: each additional work qubit multiplies the gate count by roughly 4–5×, consistent with the exponential cost of decomposing larger permutation unitaries into native two-qubit gates. Three things to notice: First, N = 15 is the only semiprime whose circuit fits within the hardware reliability window, and even there the 11.3% survival probability means roughly 9 out of 10 shots are corrupted by at least one gate error. This is why our N = 15 run showed only marginal quantum signal. Second, the gate counts grow exponentially with the number of work qubits, not with N itself. All 8-bit semiprimes 143, 221, 247, 253 require approximately the same number of gates ~2.5 million, because they all need 8 work qubits. The specific value of N matters only insofar as it determines the multiplier values, which affect how efficiently the transpiler can decompose each controlled-U gate. Third, N = 221 — cited in several recent publications as the frontier of quantum factoring — requires an estimated 2.5 million two-qubit gates: 500 times the Heron r2’s reliability limit. No amount of error mitigation, qubit selection, or transpiler optimization can rescue a circuit that is 500× too deep. If those publications report successful factoring of N = 221 on similar hardware, the result is coming from the classical post-processing, not from quantum period-finding. The honest answer: N = 15 is the largest number that current quantum hardware can factor with genuine quantum contribution, under the standard textbook QPE approach with permutation oracles. In these runs, under this textbook-QPE-with-permutation-oracles setup and these metrics, N=15 is the only case showing even marginal non-random enrichment without visible period structure. This statement comes with the caveat that N = 15 uses a hand-optimized SWAP-based oracle that is available only because of the special binary structure of 15, and that even the N = 15 result shows only marginal quantum signal 1.88× enrichment over random baseline, no visible period structure in the histogram. For N ≥ 21, the hardware output is noise. What the Literature Says: A History of Experimental Factoring The Pioneering Demonstration: N = 15 2001 The first experimental implementation of Shor’s algorithm was performed at the IBM Almaden Research Center by Vandersypen, Steffen, Breyta, Yannoni, Sherwood, and Chuang. Published in Nature in December 2001https://www.nature.com/articles/414883a, they factored 15 = 3 × 5 using a seven-qubit liquid-state nuclear magnetic resonance NMR quantum computer. The circuit was realized with approximately 300 spin selective radio frequency pulses. While NMR quantum computers were not a scalable path forward, the experiment was a landmark proof of principle. Photonic and Trapped-Ion Demonstrations 2007–2016 After the IBM NMR result, several groups demonstrated compiled versions of Shor’s algorithm on photonic platforms. Lanyon et al. 2007https://www.scribd.com/document/932312927/Lanyon-Et-Al-2007-Experimental-Demonstration-of-Shor-s-Algorithm-Wit and Lu et al. 2007https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.99.250504 independently used photonic qubits to factor 15, with important caveats: both used compiled circuits that leveraged prior knowledge of the answer. In 2012, Martín-López et al.https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.4147 demonstrated qubit recycling — an iterative approach using only a single photonic qubit that was measured and reused. That same year, Lucero et al. factored 15https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.5707 using a Josephson phase qubit. A significant milestone came in 2016, when Monz et al. demonstrated a scalable implementation of Shor’s algorithmhttps://arxiv.org/abs/1507.08852 using trapped-ion qubits, also factoring 15 but with a circuit architecture designed to generalize to larger numbers. N = 21 on IBM Processors 2021 Skosana and Tame published a proof-of-concept demonstration in Scientific Reports 2021 factoring 21 = 3× 7 on IBM quantum processors using only five qubitshttps://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-021-95973-w. Their approach used a compiled version of the quantum phase estimation routine with approximate Toffoli gates that preserved functional correctness. They also verified entanglement between the control and work register qubits, a necessary condition for the algorithm’s quantum speedup. Their results, published as part of the ICTIS 2025 conference proceedings, highlight the stark contrast between ideal and noisy execution — noise-free simulations succeeded readily while real hardware results were significantly degraded by decoherence. They implemented Shor’s algorithm to factor 221 = 13 × 17 using IBM’s quantum resources and the Qiskit framework. The paper examines success probability and performance limitations on noisy hardware, representing what appears to be the current practical frontier for Shor’s algorithm on IBM systems. Important Caveats A critical observation, noted by multiple researchers: nearly all experimental demonstrations of Shor’s algorithm on real hardware use compiled circuits that are optimized using prior knowledge of the answer. The modular exponentiation operator, the most expensive part of the circuit, is typically implemented as a pre-computed permutation matrix rather than a generic arithmetic circuit. This means the “quantum” computation is partly doing classical work in disguise. A fully generic, scalable implementation of Shor’s algorithm that doesn’t use any prior knowledge of the factors remains an open challenge for the NISQ hardware. The noise levels are simply too high for the deep circuits that generic modular arithmetic requires. The Implementation Code Architecture The implementation is split into four modules, each handling one stage of the pipeline. This section walks through the engineering decisions and, more importantly, what those decisions reveal about the gap between textbook Shor and real hardware. The Oracle: Modular Multiplication modexp.py The quantum heart of Shor’s algorithm is the modular exponentiation operator: given integers a and N, build a unitary that maps |x⟩ → |a·x mod N⟩. In a textbook presentation, this operator is constructed from reversible adders and modular arithmetic circuits. In practice, on NISQ hardware, nobody does that. Many toy-scale demonstrations, including mine, of Shor’s algorithm on real hardware, from Vandersypen’s 2001 NMR experiment factoring 15 to the recent claims of factoring 221, use what amounts to a lookup table: compute the permutation that a·x mod N induces on the computational basis states, build the corresponding permutation matrix, and hand it to the transpiler as a UnitaryGate. My implementation does the same. This is the right engineering choice and also the most important caveat. The oracle is a classically precomputed permutation matrix. We know the full multiplication table of a modulo N before we ever touch the quantum hardware. The quantum computer’s job is to find the period of this permutation using phase estimation. The oracle construction itself does not use any quantum advantage. For N = 15 specifically, I implemented hand-optimized SWAP-based circuits the buildmod15rotationgate path that exploit the fact that multiplication by 2, 4, and 8 modulo 15 are just cyclic bit rotations. These produce much shallower circuits than decomposing a 16×16 unitary gate. For all other N, the code falls back to the exact permutation matrix, which the transpiler then decomposes into native gates. This decomposition is where gate counts explode. The key numbers: a permutation gate on n qubits produces a 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ dense complex matrix. For n = 4 N = 15, that is a 16×16 matrix: 4 KiB. For n = 8 N = 221, it is 256×256: 1 MiB. For n = 10 N = 1007, it is 1024×1024: 16 MiB. Each of these then needs to be controlled on a counting qubit, doubling the matrix dimension. Memory is not the bottleneck for the sizes we care about, but transpilation cost is. Decomposing a controlled 256×256 unitary into native CX + single-qubit gates produces tens of thousands of two-qubit gates. Phase Estimation qpe.py The QPE circuit follows the textbook structure: 1. Initialize the work register to |1⟩ by flipping work\0\. Qiskit uses little-endian bit ordering, so work\0\ is the least-significant bit. 2. Apply Hadamard gates to all counting qubits. 3. For each counting qubit j = 0, 1, …, t−1, apply a controlled-U^2^j operation, where U is the modular multiplication gate. The multiplier for each controlled gate is a^2^j mod N, which is computed classically. 4. Apply the inverse QFT to the counting register, without final swaps. The no-swap inverse QFT is a deliberate choice. The textbook QFT includes swap gates at the end to reverse the qubit ordering, but these swaps add unnecessary depth. Instead, the measurement results may come out in reversed bit order. The post-processing layer handles this by testing both interpretations of each bitstring. A practical optimization: the code caches controlled oracle gates by their effective multiplier. If two different exponent indices produce the same value of a^2^j mod N, the same gate object is reused. For bases with small multiplicative orders, this avoids redundant unitary decompositions. Post-Processing postprocess.py This is where the subtlety lives, and where honest reporting requires the most care. Given a measurement outcome y from the t\-bit counting register, the textbook procedure is: compute the phase estimate y/2^t, apply the continued-fraction algorithm to find a rational approximation p/q with small denominator, and test whether q or a divisor of q is the multiplicative order of a modulo N. My implementation adds one standard improvement and applies two layers of strictness. The improvement: after recovering candidate denominators from continued fractions, test small multiples kq for k = 2, 3, 4. This handles the case where QPE returned a phase s/r with gcds, r 1. In that situation, the continued-fraction denominator is r/gcds,r rather than the true order r. Testing a few small multiples often recovers the true order. This is a legitimate algorithmic improvement described in the standard references. The strictness: only convergents that satisfy the QPE approximation bound |y/2^t − p/q| < 1/2·2^t are promoted to candidate denominators. This prevents the multiples expansion from turning every convergent into a fishing expedition. Without this filter, the pipeline becomes so permissive that it can extract factors from random bitstrings, which defeats the purpose of running a quantum computer. Even with these controls, the post-processing is powerful. For small N with small multiplicative orders, the false-positive rate the probability that a uniformly random bitstring yields valid factors through the strict pipeline can be significant. For N = 15 with a = 7, the strict-layer false-positive rate is about 5.8%. For N = 35 with a = 4, it drops to about 1.1%. Reporting these baselines is essential for interpreting the hardware results. Runtime and Error Mitigation runtime.py The hardware execution layer manages IBM credential rotation, backend selection, and two forms of error mitigation: Dynamical decoupling DD inserts compensating pulse sequences during idle periods in the circuit. I use the XpXm sequence, which is effective against low-frequency noise. This is free in the sense that it does not add to the circuit’s logical depth. Gate and measurement twirling randomize the noise channel so that errors are more uniform and predictable. This does not reduce the total error rate but makes the errors easier to characterize and mitigate. Both are enabled by default through the Qiskit Runtime SamplerV2 options. They are standard best practice for any hardware execution on IBM systems and do not constitute “cheating” in any meaningful sense. What I did not implement: full measurement error mitigation M3/TREX, zero-noise extrapolation, or probabilistic error cancellation. These would improve the signal for shallow circuits but cannot rescue circuits that are fundamentally too deep for the hardware. Experimental scope and setup These hardware results are not an exhaustive sweep over Shor’s algorithm. For each tested composite N, I chose one coprime base an and ran the corresponding circuit with 1024 shots. So the goal here is not to prove an absolute best-case or worst-case performance for each N that will come later, but to measure what a realistic, representative Shor run looks like on current hardware. That caveat matters. The order-finding subroutine depends on the chosen base, and some bases are more forgiving than others. A larger study would sweep across many valid a values and compare their output distributions. This post does not do that. It asks a narrower question: when you build a complete Shor pipeline, transpile it to real hardware, and run representative instances honestly, what survives? The Hardware Results What Counts as Success? Before presenting any results, I need to define what “success” means. This turns out to be the most important part of the entire analysis, because the choice of success metric can make the same experiment look like a triumph or a failure. Previous Shor implementations, including all the published demonstrations I surveyed, typically report success if at least one bitstring among the most frequently observed outcomes yields valid factors through classical post-processing. I call this factor\found\in\histogram: scan the top-k most common measurement outcomes, try continued-fraction postprocessing on each, and report success if any of them work. The problem with this metric is that it conflates “the quantum hardware produced useful output” with “the classical post-processing is powerful enough to find factors in noisy data.” For small N, the post-processing pipeline has a significant false-positive rate. If you scan 20 bitstrings and each one has a ~5% chance of yielding factors even under uniform random input, the probability of at least one success is 1 − 0.95²⁰ ≈ 64%. You would “succeed” most of the time even without a quantum computer. I report three metrics instead: Top-1 success: Does the single most frequently observed bitstring yield valid factors through strict quality-filtered, bounded-multiples postprocessing? This is the strongest individual-outcome test. If the quantum computer is producing meaningful output, the most common measurement should be near an ideal QPE peak, and that peak should resolve to a useful phase. Per-shot factor yield vs. null baseline: What fraction of all 1,024 shots individually yield valid factors? Compare this against the false-positive rate of the same postprocessing pipeline applied to uniformly random bitstrings. If the hardware yield significantly exceeds the random baseline, the hardware distribution is genuinely enriched. Ideal-peak overlap: Classically compute the true order r of a modulo N, then calculate where the ideal QPE peaks should appear: y ≈ s · 2^t / r for s = 0, 1, …, r−1. Measure how much of the observed shot mass falls near these predicted peak locations, compared to what uniform noise would produce. This directly tests whether the hardware output reflects the correct period, which is the entire point of the quantum computation. These three metrics answer increasingly demanding questions: did the post-processing find factors? Is the hardware output better than random? Does the hardware output actually show the right period? The Runs I executed Shor’s algorithm on IBM Quantum hardware for three semiprimes: N = 15 the classic benchmark, N = 21, and N = 35. N = 15 a = 7: 727 Two-Qubit Gates on ibm\torino This is the only run where the circuit is plausibly within the hardware’s reliability window. With 727 two-qubit gates on the 133-qubit Heron r1 processor, the expected survival probability is roughly 1 − 0.003⁷²⁷ ≈ 11%. That is low but nonzero: we might see some signal mixed with a lot of noise. The results confirm this. The strict per-shot factor yield is 10.8%, compared to a strict null baseline of 5.8%. The hardware yield is 1.88 times the random baseline: a real but modest enrichment. The quantum hardware is producing an output distribution that is somewhat better than random noise at generating factor-yielding bitstrings. However, the top-1 bitstring the single most common outcome, observed 12 times out of 1024 does not yield factors under strict postprocessing. With 253 unique outcomes across 1024 shots, the distribution is broadly spread. And the ideal-peak overlap analysis shows that the fraction of shot mass near the theoretical QPE peak locations equals the uniform-noise expectation exactly: 4.7% observed versus 4.7% expected. The hardware output does not show visible period structure. The honest summary: at 727 gates, some quantum signal survives. It manifests as a modest enrichment in the fraction of factor-yielding bitstrings 1.88x above random but not as recognizable period structure in the histogram. The circuit is too noisy to produce clean QPE peaks, but not so noisy that the output is perfectly random. N = 21 a = 19: 23,054 Two-Qubit Gates on ibm\torino This circuit is roughly 4.6 times beyond the Heron processor’s reliable gate limit. The expected survival probability is 1 − 0.003²³⁰⁵⁴ — a number so small it rounds to zero. The factor yield data confirms this. The strict yield is 4.0% against a 2.2% baseline, giving a 1.82x ratio. The ideal-peak enrichment is 1.0x: the mass near peaks matches the uniform expectation exactly. The histogram is indistinguishable from noise. Yet under the old scanning metric without quality filtering, this run ‘succeeds.’ The most common bitstring observed 6 times out of 1024 itself yields factors through the unfiltered continued-fraction pipeline, because the convergent denominator 6 happens to be the true order, even though the approximation error is 5× above the strict quality threshold. This illustrates exactly why the quality filter matters: without it, numerically coincidental convergents get promoted into valid-looking results. N = 35 a = 4: 116,706 Two-Qubit Gates on ibm\fez This circuit has 116,706 two-qubit gates — roughly 23 times the hardware’s reliability limit. It was submitted primarily to establish the baseline behavior of a completely noise-dominated circuit. The strict yield is 2.9% against a 1.1% baseline, giving a 2.6x ratio. This is the highest ratio among the three runs, which might seem surprising. But with only 1024 shots across 4096 possible outcomes, the statistical uncertainty is large. The ideal-peak enrichment is 1.56x, slightly above uniform but well within what noise fluctuations can produce. The exploratory-layer analysis reveals the real story: with unbounded continued-fraction expansion, every single shot 100% yields valid factors, and the random baseline is also 100%. When the post-processing net is wide enough, it catches everything. The “success” is entirely classical. The Two-Layer Picture The most instructive result of this experiment is not any individual factoring claim. It is the contrast between the strict and exploratory postprocessing layers. The strict layer quality-filtered convergents, bounded multiples k ≤ 4 produces factor yields that are modestly above the random baseline for all three runs. The enrichment ratios range from 1.82x to 2.61x. These numbers are real, but they do not constitute compelling evidence of quantum period-finding. When Ghugare et al. report factoring N = 221 on IBM hardware, or when Saxena et al. report N = 91, what success metric did they use? If they used top-k histogram scanning with aggressive continued-fraction postprocessing which the methodology sections of both papers suggest, then the same questions apply: what is the false-positive rate? When the classical postprocessing pipeline has a significant false-positive rate, “found factors” and “the quantum computer found factors” are different claims. Distinguishing them requires the kind of null-baseline and peak-overlap analysis described here. The Honest Answer The biggest number that current quantum hardware can factor with genuine quantum contribution is, at most, N = 15. Even for N = 15, the evidence is marginal: a 1.88x enrichment in factor yield over the random baseline, with no visible period structure in the histogram. Numbers larger than 15 can be “factored” in the sense that classical postprocessing of noisy quantum output can recover factors. But the same postprocessing would recover factors from random input at a comparable rate. The quantum hardware is not doing the work. This is a disappointing answer if you were hoping for a dramatic factoring demonstration. But it is the scientifically honest one. And the picture it paints — of a technology that produces genuine but fragile quantum signal at very shallow circuit depths, rapidly overwhelmed by noise as circuits get deeper — is exactly what the NISQ era looks like from the inside. So in the end, the title is not just a joke. Sometimes it’s too slow… for Shor. The mathematics is elegant, the algorithm is revolutionary, and the cryptographic stakes are enormous, but the hardware is not there yet. Running this experiment on IBM’s Heron processors did not reveal a machine ready to threaten RSA. It revealed something more grounded and, in its own way, more important: where the edge actually is. Today, that edge sits uncomfortably close to N = 15. At 727 two-qubit gates, there is a faint quantum signal — a 1.88× enrichment in factor yield over random noise. At 23,000 gates, the signal is gone. The algorithm works. The physics works. The engineering is not there yet. But this experiment also revealed something about the field itself. The metrics we use to evaluate quantum factoring are not keeping pace with the hardware claims being made. A top-20 histogram scan with aggressive continued-fraction expansion can “find factors” in pure noise. An unbounded multiples expansion can turn every bitstring into a success. These are not quantum results , they are classical artifacts dressed in quantum clothing. Until the community adopts honest baselines, peak-overlap analysis, and two-layer reporting as standard practice, every published claim of “factoring N on a quantum computer” deserves a raised eyebrow and a request for the raw histogram. Shor’s algorithm changed the future the moment it was discovered. But in the present, the future is still arriving one noisy gate at a time. This post is the first in a series. The next installment applies the metrics developed here to every published experimental Shor result — from Vandersypen’s 2001 NMR factoring of 15 to the recent claims of 91 and 221 on IBM hardware, and the adiabatic “stunt” factorizations that have been inflating the field’s headline numbers for a decade. If those experiments cannot survive a null-baseline comparison and a peak-overlap test, the largest number genuinely factored by quantum period-finding may be even smaller than you think.
